<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>A function $$f$$ consists of a set of inputs, a set of outputs, and a rule for assigning each input to exactly one output. The set of inputs is called the domain of the function. The set of outputs is called the range of the function.</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="1.1" title="Evaluating Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For the function $$f(x) = 3x^{2} + 2x - 1,$$ evaluate</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(-2)$$</item>
        <item>$$f\left( \sqrt{2} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$f(a + h)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Substitute the given value for x in the formula for $$f(x).$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(-2) = 3(-2)^{2} + 2(-2) - 1 = 12 - 4 - 1 = 7$$</item>
        <item>$$f\left( \sqrt{2} \right) = 3\left( \sqrt{2} \right)^{2} + 2\sqrt{2} - 1 = 6 + 2\sqrt{2} - 1 = 5 + 2\sqrt{2}$$</item>
        <item>$$\begin{array}{cl} {f\left( {a + h} \right) = 3\left( {a + h} \right)^{2} + 2\left( {a + h} \right) - 1} & {= 3\left( {a^{2} + 2ah + h^{2}} \right) + 2a + 2h - 1} \\ & {= 3a^{2} + 6ah + 3h^{2} + 2a + 2h - 1} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

title: Finding Domain and Range
snippet: Finding Domain and Range: For each of the following functions, determine the i. domain and ii. range. f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} + 5 f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 2} - 1 f(x) = \frac{3}{x - 2} Consider f(x) = \left( {x - 4} \right)^{2} + 5. Since f(x) = {(x...
body_xml:
<example number="1.2" title="Finding Domain and Range">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following functions, determine the i. domain and ii. range.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} + 5$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 2} - 1$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \frac{3}{x - 2}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Consider $$f(x) = \left( {x - 4} \right)^{2} + 5.$$ Since $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} + 5$$ is a real number for any real number $$x,$$ the domain of $$f$$ is the interval $$(-\infty,\infty).$$ Since $${(x - 4)}^{2} \geq 0,$$ we know $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} + 5 \geq 5.$$ Therefore, the range must be a subset of $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq 5 \right\}.$$ To show that every element in this set is in the range, we need to show that for a given $$y$$ in that set, there is a real number $$x$$ such that $$f(x) = {(x - 4)}^{2} + 5 = y.$$ Solving this equation for $$x,$$ we see that we need $$x$$ such that $${(x - 4)}^{2} = y - 5.$$ This equation is satisfied as long as there exists a real number $$x$$ such that $$x - 4 = \pm \sqrt{y - 5}.$$ Since $$y \geq 5,$$ the square root is well-defined. We conclude that for $$x = 4 \pm \sqrt{y - 5},f(x) = y,$$ and therefore the range is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq 5 \right\}.$$</item>
        <item>Consider $$f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 2} - 1.$$ To find the domain of $$f,$$ we need the expression $$3x + 2 \geq 0.$$ Solving this inequality, we conclude that the domain is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \geq -2/3 \right\}.$$ To find the range of $$f,$$ we note that since $$\sqrt{3x + 2} \geq 0,f(x) = \sqrt{3x + 2} - 1 \geq -1.$$ Therefore, the range of $$f$$ must be a subset of the set $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq -1 \right\}.$$ To show that every element in this set is in the range of $$f,$$ we need to show that for all $$y$$ in this set, there exists a real number $$x$$ in the domain such that $$f(x) = y.$$ Let $$y \geq -1.$$ Then, $$f(x) = y$$ if and only if $$\sqrt{3x + 2} - 1 = y.$$ Solving this equation for $$x,$$ we see that $$x$$ must solve the equation $$\sqrt{3x + 2} = y + 1.$$ Since $$y \geq -1,$$ such an $$x$$ could exist. Squaring both sides of this equation, we have $$3x + 2 = {(y + 1)}^{2}.$$ Therefore, we need $$3x = {(y + 1)}^{2} - 2,$$ which implies $$x = \frac{1}{3}\left( {y + 1} \right)^{2} - \frac{2}{3}.$$ We just need to verify that $$x$$ is in the domain of $$f.$$ Since the domain of $$f$$ consists of all real numbers greater than or equal to $$-2/3,$$ and $$\frac{1}{3}\left( {y + 1} \right)^{2} - \frac{2}{3} \geq - \frac{2}{3},$$ there does exist an $$x$$ in the domain of $$f.$$ We conclude that the range of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq -1 \right\}.$$</item>
        <item>Consider $$f(x) = 3/(x - 2).$$ Since $$3/(x - 2)$$ is defined when the denominator is nonzero, the domain is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 2 \right\}.$$ To find the range of $$f,$$ we need to find the values of $$y$$ such that there exists a real number $$x$$ in the domain with the property that $$\frac{3}{x - 2} = y.$$ Solving this equation for $$x,$$ we find that $$x = \frac{3}{y} + 2.$$ Therefore, as long as $$y \neq 0,$$ there exists a real number $$x$$ in the domain such that $$f(x) = y.$$ Thus, the range is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \neq 0 \right\}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph>Given a function $$f,$$ every vertical line that may be drawn intersects the graph of $$f$$ no more than once. If any vertical line intersects a set of points more than once, the set of points does not represent a function.</paragraph>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: We say that a function f is increasing on the interval I if for all x_{1},x_{2} \in I, f(x_{1}) \leq f(x_{2}) \text{when} x_{1} < x_{2}. We say f is strictly increasing on the interval I if for all x_{1},x_{2} \in I, f(x_{1}) <...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>We say that a function $$f$$ is increasing on the interval $$I$$ if for all $$x_{1},x_{2} \in I,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x_{1}) \leq f(x_{2}) \text{when} x_{1} < x_{2}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We say $$f$$ is strictly increasing on the interval $$I$$ if for all $$x_{1},x_{2} \in I,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x_{1}) < f(x_{2}) \text{when} x_{1} < x_{2}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We say that a function $$f$$ is decreasing on the interval $$I$$ if for all $$x_{1},x_{2} \in I,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x_{1}) \geq f(x_{2}) \text{if} x_{1} < x_{2}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We say that a function $$f$$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $$I$$ if for all $$x_{1},x_{2} \in I,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x_{1}) > f(x_{2}) \text{if} x_{1} < x_{2}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Combining Functions Using Mathematical Operations
snippet: Combining Functions Using Mathematical Operations: Given the functions f(x) = 2x - 3 and g(x) = x^{2} - 1, find each of the following functions and state its domain. (f + g)(x) (f - g)(x) (f \cdot g)(x) \left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x) \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="1.6" title="Combining Functions Using Mathematical Operations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Given the functions $$f(x) = 2x - 3$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2} - 1,$$ find each of the following functions and state its domain.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$(f + g)(x)$$</item>
        <item>$$(f - g)(x)$$</item>
        <item>$$(f \cdot g)(x)$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\left( {f + g} \right)(x) = \left( {2x - 3} \right) + {({x^{2} - 1})} = x^{2} + 2x - 4.$$ The domain of this function is the interval $$\left( {-\infty,\infty} \right).$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {f - g} \right)(x) = \left( {2x - 3} \right) - {({x^{2} - 1})} = -x^{2} + 2x - 2.$$ The domain of this function is the interval $$\left( {-\infty,\infty} \right).$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( {f \cdot g} \right)(x) = \left( {2x - 3} \right){({x^{2} - 1})} = 2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 2x + 3.$$ The domain of this function is the interval $$\left( {-\infty,\infty} \right).$$</item>
        <item>$$\left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x) = \frac{2x - 3}{x^{2} - 1}.$$ The domain of this function is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq \text{±} 1 \right\}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Compositions of Functions Defined by Formulas
snippet: Compositions of Functions Defined by Formulas: Consider the functions f(x) = x^{2} + 1 and g(x) = 1/x. Find (g \circ f)(x) and state its domain and range. Evaluate (g \circ f)(4),(g \circ f)(-1/2). Find (f \circ g)(x) and state its domain...
body_xml:
<example number="1.7" title="Compositions of Functions Defined by Formulas">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the functions $$f(x) = x^{2} + 1$$ and $$g(x) = 1/x.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find $$(g \circ f)(x)$$ and state its domain and range.</item>
        <item>Evaluate $$(g \circ f)(4),(g \circ f)(-1/2).$$</item>
        <item>Find $$(f \circ g)(x)$$ and state its domain and range.</item>
        <item>Evaluate $$(f \circ g)(4),(f \circ g)(-1/2).$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>We can find the formula for $$(g \circ f)(x)$$ in two different ways. We could write $$(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(x^{2} + 1) = \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}.$$ Alternatively, we could write $$(g \circ f)(x) = g\left( {f(x)} \right) = \frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}.$$ Since $$x^{2} + 1 \neq 0$$ for all real numbers $$x,$$ the domain of $$(g \circ f)(x)$$ is the set of all real numbers. Since $$0 < 1/{({x^{2} + 1})} \leq 1,$$ the range is, at most, the interval $$\left( {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ To show that the range is this entire interval, we let $$y = 1/{({x^{2} + 1})}$$ and solve this equation for $$x$$ to show that for all $$y$$ in the interval $$\left( {0,1} \right\rbrack,$$ there exists a real number $$x$$ such that $$y = 1/{({x^{2} + 1})}.$$ Solving this equation for $$x,$$ we see that $$x^{2} + 1 = 1/y,$$ which implies that $$x = \pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{y} - 1}.$$ If $$y$$ is in the interval $$\left( {0,1} \right\rbrack,$$ the expression under the radical is nonnegative, and therefore there exists a real number $$x$$ such that $$1/{({x^{2} + 1})} = y.$$ We conclude that the range of $$g \circ f$$ is the interval $$\left( {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$</item>
        <item>$$(g \circ f)(4) = g(f(4)) = g(4^{2} + 1) = g(17) = \frac{1}{17}$$ $$(g \circ f)\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = g\left( {f\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} \right) = g\left( {\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2} + 1} \right) = g\left( \frac{5}{4} \right) = \frac{4}{5}$$</item>
        <item>We can find a formula for $$(f \circ g)(x)$$ in two ways. First, we could write $$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f\left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)^{2} + 1.$$ Alternatively, we could write $$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = {(g(x))}^{2} + 1 = \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)^{2} + 1.$$ The domain of $$f \circ g$$ is the set of all real numbers $$x$$ such that $$x \neq 0.$$ To find the range of $$f,$$ we need to find all values $$y$$ for which there exists a real number $$x \neq 0$$ such that $$\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)^{2} + 1 = y.$$ Solving this equation for $$x,$$ we see that we need $$x$$ to satisfy $$\left( \frac{1}{x} \right)^{2} = y - 1,$$ which simplifies to $$\frac{1}{x} = \pm \sqrt{y - 1}.$$ Finally, we obtain $$x = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{y - 1}}.$$ Since $$1/\sqrt{y - 1}$$ is a real number if and only if $$y > 1,$$ the range of $$f◦ g$$ is the set $$\left\{ y \middle| y > 1 \right\}.$$</item>
        <item>$$(f \circ g)(4) = f(g(4)) = f\left( \frac{1}{4} \right) = \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)^{2} + 1 = \frac{17}{16}$$ $$(f \circ g)\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = f\left( {g\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)} \right) = f(-2) = {(-2)}^{2} + 1 = 5$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Application Involving a Composite Function
snippet: Application Involving a Composite Function: A store is advertising a sale of 20\% off all merchandise. Caroline has a coupon that entitles her to an additional 15\% off any item, including sale merchandise. If Caroline decides to purchase...
body_xml:
<example number="1.9" title="Application Involving a Composite Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A store is advertising a sale of $$20\%$$ off all merchandise. Caroline has a coupon that entitles her to an additional $$15\%$$ off any item, including sale merchandise. If Caroline decides to purchase an item with an original price of $$x$$ dollars, how much will she end up paying if she applies her coupon to the sale price? Solve this problem by using a composite function.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the sale price is $$20\%$$ off the original price, if an item is $$x$$ dollars, its sale price is given by $$f(x) = 0.80x.$$ Since the coupon entitles an individual to $$15\%$$ off the price of any item, if an item is $$y$$ dollars, the price, after applying the coupon, is given by $$g(y) = 0.85y.$$ Therefore, if the price is originally $$x$$ dollars, its sale price will be $$f(x) = 0.80x$$ and then its final price after the coupon will be $$g(f(x)) = 0.85(0.80x) = 0.68x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

snippet: Even and Odd Functions: Determine whether each of the following functions is even, odd, or neither. f(x) = -5x^{4} + 7x^{2} - 2 f(x) = 2x^{5} - 4x + 5 f(x) = \frac{3x}{x^{2} + 1} To determine whether a function is even or odd, we evaluate...

<example number="1.10" title="Even and Odd Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Determine whether each of the following functions is even, odd, or neither.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = -5x^{4} + 7x^{2} - 2$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = 2x^{5} - 4x + 5$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \frac{3x}{x^{2} + 1}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To determine whether a function is even or odd, we evaluate $$f(-x)$$ and compare it to f(x) and $$-f(x).$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f\left( {-x} \right) = -5\left( {-x} \right)^{4} + 7\left( {-x} \right)^{2} - 2 = -5x^{4} + 7x^{2} - 2 = f(x).$$ Therefore, $$f$$ is even.</item>
        <item>$$f(-x) = 2{(-x)}^{5} - 4(-x) + 5 = -2x^{5} + 4x + 5.$$ Now, $$f\left( {-x} \right) \neq f(x).$$ Furthermore, noting that $$-f(x) = -2x^{5} + 4x - 5,$$ we see that $$f\left( {-x} \right) \neq -f(x).$$ Therefore, $$f$$ is neither even nor odd.</item>
        <item>$$f(-x) = 3(-x)/(\left( {-x} \right)^{2} + 1) = -3x/(x^{2} + 1) = -\lbrack 3x/(x^{2} + 1)\rbrack = -f(x).$$ Therefore, $$f$$ is odd.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Working with the Absolute Value Function
snippet: Working with the Absolute Value Function: Find the domain and range of the function \left. f(x) = 2 \middle| x - 3 \middle| + 4. \right. Since the absolute value function is defined for all real numbers, the domain of this function is...
body_xml:
<example number="1.11" title="Working with the Absolute Value Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the domain and range of the function $$\left. f(x) = 2 \middle| x - 3 \middle| + 4. \right.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since the absolute value function is defined for all real numbers, the domain of this function is $$(-\infty,\infty).$$ Since $$\left| x - 3 \middle| \geq 0 \right.$$ for all $$x,$$ the function $$\left. f(x) = 2 \middle| x - 3 \middle| + 4 \geq 4. \right.$$ Therefore, the range is, at most, the set $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq 4 \right\}.$$ To see that the range is, in fact, this whole set, we need to show that for $$y \geq 4$$ there exists a real number $$x$$ such that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. 2 \middle| x - 3 \middle| + 4 = y. \right.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>A real number $$x$$ satisfies this equation as long as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$|x - 3| = \frac{1}{2}(y - 4).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$y \geq 4,$$ we know $$y - 4 \geq 0,$$ and thus the right-hand side of the equation is nonnegative, so it is possible that there is a solution. Furthermore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$|x - 3| = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {- (x - 3) \text{if} x < 3} \\ {x - 3 \text{if} x \geq 3} \end{matrix} \right..$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, we see there are two solutions:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x = \pm \frac{1}{2}(y - 4) + 3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The range of this function is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geq 4 \right\}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: A Linear Distance Function: Jessica leaves her house at 5:50 a.m. and goes for a 9-mile run. She returns to her house at 7:08 a.m. Answer the following questions, assuming Jessica runs at a constant pace. Describe the distance D (in miles)...

<example number="1.13" title="A Linear Distance Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Jessica leaves her house at 5:50 a.m. and goes for a 9-mile run. She returns to her house at 7:08 a.m. Answer the following questions, assuming Jessica runs at a constant pace.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Describe the distance $$D$$ (in miles) Jessica runs as a linear function of her run time $$t$$ (in minutes).</item>
        <item>Sketch a graph of $$D.$$</item>
        <item>Interpret the meaning of the slope.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>At time $$t = 0,$$ Jessica is at her house, so $$D(0) = 0.$$ At time $$t = 78$$ minutes, Jessica has finished running $$9$$ mi, so $$D(78) = 9.$$ The slope of the linear function is $$m = \frac{9 - 0}{78 - 0} = \frac{3}{26}.$$ The $$y$$ -intercept is $$\left( {0,0} \right),$$ so the equation for this linear function is $$D(t) = \frac{3}{26}t.$$</item>
        <item>To graph $$D,$$ use the fact that the graph passes through the origin and has slope $$m = 3/26.$$</item>
        <item>The slope $$m = 3/26 \approx 0.115$$ describes the distance (in miles) Jessica runs per minute, or her average velocity.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

If $$b^{2} - 4ac = 0,$$ this formula tells us there is only one solution, and it is a real number. If $$b^{2} - 4ac < 0,$$ no real numbers satisfy the quadratic equation.</paragraph>

<example number="1.14" title="Graphing Polynomial Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For the following functions a. and b., i. describe the behavior of $$f(x)$$ as $$x\rightarrow \text{±} \infty,$$ ii. find all zeros of $$f,$$ and iii. sketch a graph of $$f.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = -2x^{2} + 4x - 1$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 4x$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The function $$f(x) = -2x^{2} + 4x - 1$$ is a quadratic function. Because $$a = -2 < 0, \text{as} x\rightarrow \text{±} \infty,f(x)\rightarrow \text{−∞.}$$ To find the zeros of $$f,$$ use the quadratic formula. The zeros are $$x = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{4^{2} - 4(-2)(-1)}}{2(-2)} = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{8}}{-4} = \frac{-4 \pm 2\sqrt{2}}{-4} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{2}}{2}.$$ To sketch the graph of $$f,$$ use the information from your previous answers and combine it with the fact that the graph is a parabola opening downward.</item>
        <item>The function $$f(x) = x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 4x$$ is a cubic function. Because $$a = 1 > 0, \text{as} x\rightarrow\infty,f(x)\rightarrow\infty.$$ As $$x\rightarrow \text{−∞} ,f(x)\rightarrow \text{−∞} .$$ To find the zeros of $$f,$$ we need to factor the polynomial. First, when we factor $$x$$ out of all the terms, we find $$f(x) = x(x^{2} - 3x - 4).$$ Then, when we factor the quadratic function $$x^{2} - 3x - 4,$$ we find $$f(x) = x(x - 4)(x + 1).$$ Therefore, the zeros of $$f$$ are $$x = 0,4,-1.$$ Combining the results from parts i. and ii., draw a rough sketch of $$f.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Maximizing Revenue: A company is interested in predicting the amount of revenue it will receive depending on the price it charges for a particular item. Using the data from Table 1.6, the company arrives at the following quadratic function...
body_xml:
<example number="1.15" title="Maximizing Revenue">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A company is interested in predicting the amount of revenue it will receive depending on the price it charges for a particular item. Using the data from Table 1.6, the company arrives at the following quadratic function to model revenue $$R$$ (in thousands of dollars) as a function of price per item $$p:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$R(p) = p \cdot \left( {-1.04p + 26} \right) = -1.04p^{2} + 26p$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>for $$0 \leq p \leq 25.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Predict the revenue if the company sells the item at a price of $$p = \$5$$ and $$p = \$17.$$</item>
        <item>Find the zeros of this function and interpret the meaning of the zeros.</item>
        <item>Sketch a graph of $$R.$$</item>
        <item>Use the graph to determine the value of $$p$$ that maximizes revenue. Find the maximum revenue.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Evaluating the revenue function at $$p = 5$$ and $$p = 17,$$ we can conclude that $$\begin{array}{l} \\ {R(5) = -1.04{(5)}^{2} + 26(5) = 104, \text{so revenue} = \text{\$104,000;} } \\ {R(17) = -1.04{(17)}^{2} + 26(17) = 141.44, \text{so revenue} = \text{\$141,440.} } \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>The zeros of this function can be found by solving the equation $$-1.04p^{2} + 26p = 0.$$ When we factor the quadratic expression, we get $$p\left( {-1.04p + 26} \right) = 0.$$ The solutions to this equation are given by $$p = 0,25.$$ For these values of $$p,$$ the revenue is zero. When $$p = \$0,$$ the revenue is zero because the company is giving away its merchandise for free. When $$p = \$25,$$ the revenue is zero because the price is too high, and no one will buy any items.</item>
        <item>Knowing the fact that the function is quadratic, we also know the graph is a parabola. Since the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. One property of parabolas is that they are symmetric about the axis, so since the zeros are at $$p = 0$$ and $$p = 25,$$ the parabola must be symmetric about the line halfway between them, or $$p = 12.5.$$</item>
        <item>The function is a parabola with zeros at $$p = 0$$ and $$p = 25,$$ and it is symmetric about the line $$p = 12.5,$$ so the maximum revenue occurs at a price of $$p = \$12.50$$ per item. At that price, the revenue is $$R(p) = -1.04(12.5)^{2} + 26(12.5) = \$162,500.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding Domain and Range for Algebraic Functions
snippet: Finding Domain and Range for Algebraic Functions: For each of the following functions, find the domain and range. f(x) = \frac{3x - 1}{5x + 2} f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^{2}} It is not possible to divide by zero, so the domain is the set of real...
body_xml:
<example number="1.16" title="Finding Domain and Range for Algebraic Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following functions, find the domain and range.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = \frac{3x - 1}{5x + 2}$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>It is not possible to divide by zero, so the domain is the set of real numbers $$x$$ such that $$x \neq -2/5.$$ To find the range, we need to find the values $$y$$ for which there exists a real number $$x$$ such that $$y = \frac{3x - 1}{5x + 2}.$$ When we multiply both sides of this equation by $$5x + 2,$$ we see that $$x$$ must satisfy the equation $$5xy + 2y = 3x - 1.$$ From this equation, we can see that $$x$$ must satisfy $$2y + 1 = x(3 - 5y).$$ If $$y = 3/5,$$ this equation has no solution. On the other hand, as long as $$y \neq 3/5,$$ $$x = \frac{2y + 1}{3 - 5y}$$ satisfies this equation. We can conclude that the range of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \neq 3/5 \right\}.$$</item>
        <item>To find the domain of $$f$$ , we need to identify values of $$x$$ with $$4 - x^{2} \geq 0$$ . Note that $$4 - x^{2} = 0$$ when $$x = 2$$ or $$x = - 2$$ . Solving $$4 - x^{2} > 0$$ is equivalent to solving $$(2 - x)(2 + x) > 0$$ . If this inequality is true, then both factors are positive or both are negative. Case 1: Both factors are positive. $$2 - x > 0 \text{and} 2 + x > 0$$ $$x < 2 \text{and} x > - 2$$ So, the expression $$4 - x^{2}$$ is positive for all values in the interval $$- 2 < x < 2$$ . Case 2: Both factors are negative. $$2 - x < 0 \text{and} 2 + x < 0$$ $$x > 2 \text{and} x < - 2$$ There is no value of $$x$$ that can satisfy both inequalities. The domain of the function is $$\left\{ x \middle| - 2 \leq x \leq 2 \right\}$$ . To identify the range, note that if $$- 2 \leq x \leq 2$$ , then $$0 \leq 4 - x^{2} \leq 4$$ . Therefore, $$0 \leq \sqrt{4 - x^{2}} \leq 2$$ . The range of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| 0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}$$ .</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="1.20" title="Parking Fees Described by a Piecewise-Defined Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In a big city, drivers are charged variable rates for parking in a parking garage. They are charged \$10 for the first hour or any part of the first hour and an additional \$2 for each hour or part thereof up to a maximum of \$30 for the day. The parking garage is open from 6 a.m. to 12 midnight.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Write a piecewise-defined function that describes the cost $$C$$ to park in the parking garage as a function of hours parked $$x.$$</item>
        <item>Sketch a graph of this function $$C(x).$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Since the parking garage is open 18 hours each day, the domain for this function is $$\left. \text{\{} x \middle| 0 < x \leq 18 \right\}.$$ The cost to park a car at this parking garage can be described piecewise by the function $$C(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {10,0 < x \leq 1} \\ {12,1 < x \leq 2} \\ {14,2 < x \leq 3} \\ {16,3 < x \leq 4} \\ \vdots \\ {30,10 < x \leq 18} \end{matrix} \right..$$</item>
        <item>The graph of the function consists of several horizontal line segments.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$P = (x,y)$$ be a point on the unit circle centered at the origin $$O.$$ Let $$\theta$$ be an angle with an initial side along the positive $$x$$ -axis and a terminal side given by the line segment $$OP.$$ The trigonometric functions are then defined as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} {\sin \theta = y} & & & {\csc \theta = \frac{1}{y}} \\ {\cos \theta = x} & & & {\sec \theta = \frac{1}{x}} \\ {\tan \theta = \frac{y}{x}} & & & {\cot \theta = \frac{x}{y}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If $$x = 0,\sec \theta$$ and $$\tan \theta$$ are undefined. If $$y = 0,$$ then $$\cot \theta$$ and $$\csc \theta$$ are undefined.</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Evaluating Trigonometric Functions: Evaluate each of the following expressions. \sin \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) \cos \left( {- \frac{5\pi}{6}} \right) \tan \left( \frac{15\pi}{4} \right) On the unit circle, the angle \theta =...

<example number="1.23" title="Evaluating Trigonometric Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate each of the following expressions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\sin \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\cos \left( {- \frac{5\pi}{6}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\tan \left( \frac{15\pi}{4} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>On the unit circle, the angle $$\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$$ corresponds to the point $$\left( {- \frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right).$$ Therefore, $$\sin \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right) = y = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$</item>
        <item>An angle $$\theta = - \frac{5\pi}{6}$$ corresponds to a revolution in the negative direction, as shown. Therefore, $$\cos \left( {- \frac{5\pi}{6}} \right) = x = - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$$</item>
        <item>An angle $$\theta = \frac{15\pi}{4} = 2\pi + \frac{7\pi}{4}.$$ Therefore, this angle corresponds to more than one revolution, as shown. Knowing the fact that an angle of $$\frac{7\pi}{4}$$ corresponds to the point $$\left( {\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}} \right),$$ we can conclude that $$\tan \left( \frac{15\pi}{4} \right) = \frac{y}{x} = -1.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Rule: Trigonometric Identities: Reciprocal identities \begin{array}{lccl} {\tan \theta = \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}} & & & {\cot \theta = \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}} \\ {\csc \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta}} & & & {\sec \theta =...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Trigonometric Identities" title="Rule: Trigonometric Identities">
    <paragraph>Reciprocal identities</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lccl} {\tan \theta = \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}} & & & {\cot \theta = \frac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}} \\ {\csc \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta}} & & & {\sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Pythagorean identities</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1 1 + \tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta 1 + \cot^{2}\theta = \csc^{2}\theta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Addition and subtraction formulas</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sin \left( {\alpha \pm \beta} \right) = \sin \alpha\cos \beta \pm \cos \alpha\sin \beta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\cos (\alpha \pm \beta) = \cos \alpha\cos \beta \mp \sin \alpha\sin \beta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Double-angle formulas</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sin \left( {2\theta} \right) = 2\sin \theta\cos \theta$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\cos \left( {2\theta} \right) = 2\cos^{2}\theta - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta = \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Solving Trigonometric Equations
snippet: Solving Trigonometric Equations: For each of the following equations, use a trigonometric identity to find all solutions. 1 + \cos \left( {2\theta} \right) = \cos \theta \sin \left( {2\theta} \right) = \tan \theta Using the double-angle...
body_xml:
<example number="1.25" title="Solving Trigonometric Equations">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following equations, use a trigonometric identity to find all solutions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$1 + \cos \left( {2\theta} \right) = \cos \theta$$</item>
        <item>$$\sin \left( {2\theta} \right) = \tan \theta$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using the double-angle formula for $$\cos (2\theta),$$ we see that $$\theta$$ is a solution of $$1 + \cos (2\theta) = \cos \theta$$ if and only if $$1 + 2\cos^{2}\theta - 1 = \cos \theta,$$ which is true if and only if $$2\cos^{2}\theta - \cos \theta = 0.$$ To solve this equation, it is important to note that we need to factor the left-hand side and not divide both sides of the equation by $$\cos \theta.$$ The problem with dividing by $$\cos \theta$$ is that it is possible that $$\cos \theta$$ is zero. In fact, if we did divide both sides of the equation by $$\cos \theta,$$ we would miss some of the solutions of the original equation. Factoring the left-hand side of the equation, we see that $$\theta$$ is a solution of this equation if and only if $$\cos \theta\left( {2\cos \theta - 1} \right) = 0.$$ Since $$\cos \theta = 0$$ when $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2} \pm \pi,\frac{\pi}{2} \pm 2\pi \text{,…,}$$ and $$\cos \theta = 1/2$$ when $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{3} \pm 2\pi \text{,…} \text{or} \theta = - \frac{\pi}{3}, - \frac{\pi}{3} \pm 2\pi \text{,…,}$$ we conclude that the set of solutions to this equation is $$\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi,\theta = \frac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi, \text{and} \theta = - \frac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi,n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \text{…} .$$</item>
        <item>Using the double-angle formula for $$\sin \left( {2\theta} \right)$$ and the reciprocal identity for $$\tan (\theta),$$ the equation can be written as $$2\sin \theta\cos \theta = \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}.$$ To solve this equation, we multiply both sides by $$\cos \theta$$ to eliminate the denominator, and say that if $$\theta$$ satisfies this equation, then $$\theta$$ satisfies the equation $$2\sin \theta\cos^{2}\theta - \sin \theta = 0.$$ However, we need to be a little careful here. Even if $$\theta$$ satisfies this new equation, it may not satisfy the original equation because, to satisfy the original equation, we would need to be able to divide both sides of the equation by $$\cos \theta.$$ However, if $$\cos \theta = 0,$$ we cannot divide both sides of the equation by $$\cos \theta.$$ Therefore, it is possible that we may arrive at extraneous solutions. So, at the end, it is important to check for extraneous solutions. Returning to the equation, it is important that we factor $$\sin \theta$$ out of both terms on the left-hand side instead of dividing both sides of the equation by $$\sin \theta.$$ Factoring the left-hand side of the equation, we can rewrite this equation as $$\sin \theta(2\cos^{2}\theta - 1) = 0.$$ Therefore, the solutions are given by the angles $$\theta$$ such that $$\sin \theta = 0$$ or $$\cos^{2}\theta = 1/2.$$ The solutions of the first equation are $$\theta = 0, \pm \pi, \pm 2\pi \text{,….}$$ The solutions of the second equation are $$\theta = \pi/4,(\pi/4) \pm (\pi/2),(\pi/4) \pm \pi \text{,….}$$ After checking for extraneous solutions, the set of solutions to the equation is $$\theta = n\pi \text{and} \theta = \frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{n\pi}{2},n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \text{…} .$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="1.26" title="Proving a Trigonometric Identity">

    <solution>
      <paragraph>We start with the identity</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Dividing both sides of this equation by $$\cos^{2}\theta,$$ we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta} + 1 = \frac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$\sin \theta/\cos \theta = \tan \theta$$ and $$1/\cos \theta = \sec \theta,$$ we conclude that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\tan^{2}\theta + 1 = \sec^{2}\theta.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Given a function $$f$$ with domain $$D$$ and range $$R,$$ its inverse function (if it exists) is the function $$f^{-1}$$ with domain $$R$$ and range $$D$$ such that $$f^{-1}(y) = x$$ if $$f(x) = y.$$ In other words, for a function $$f$$ and its inverse $$f^{-1},$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{-1}\left( {f(x)} \right) = x \text{for all} x \text{in} D, \text{and} f\left( {f^{-1}(y)} \right) = y \text{for all} y \text{in} R.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="1.29" title="Finding an Inverse Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the inverse for the function $$f(x) = 3x - 4.$$ State the domain and range of the inverse function. Verify that $$f^{-1}(f(x)) = x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Follow the steps outlined in the strategy.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 1. If $$y = 3x - 4,$$ then $$3x = y + 4$$ and $$x = \frac{1}{3}y + \frac{4}{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. Rewrite as $$y = \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{4}{3}$$ and let $$y = f^{-1}(x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, $$f^{-1}(x) = \frac{1}{3}x + \frac{4}{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the domain of $$f$$ is $$(-\infty,\infty),$$ the range of $$f^{-1}$$ is $$(-\infty,\infty).$$ Since the range of $$f$$ is $$(-\infty,\infty),$$ the domain of $$f^{-1}$$ is $$(-\infty,\infty).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>You can verify that $$f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$ by writing</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{-1}(f(x)) = f^{-1}(3x - 4) = \frac{1}{3}(3x - 4) + \frac{4}{3} = x - \frac{4}{3} + \frac{4}{3} = x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Note that for $$f^{-1}(x)$$ to be the inverse of $$f(x),$$ both $$f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$$ and $$f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$$ for all x in the domain of the inside function.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Restricting the Domain: Consider the function f(x) = \left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}. Sketch the graph of f and use the horizontal line test to show that f is not one-to-one. Show that f is one-to-one on the restricted domain \lbrack-1,\infty)....
body_xml:
<example number="1.31" title="Restricting the Domain">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Consider the function $$f(x) = \left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Sketch the graph of $$f$$ and use the horizontal line test to show that $$f$$ is not one-to-one.</item>
        <item>Show that $$f$$ is one-to-one on the restricted domain $$\lbrack-1,\infty).$$ Determine the domain and range for the inverse of $$f$$ on this restricted domain and find a formula for $$f^{-1}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The graph of $$f$$ is the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ shifted left 1 unit. Since there exists a horizontal line intersecting the graph more than once, $$f$$ is not one-to-one.</item>
        <item>On the interval $${\lbrack-1,\infty),} f$$ is one-to-one. The domain and range of $$f^{-1}$$ are given by the range and domain of $$f,$$ respectively. Therefore, the domain of $$f^{-1}$$ is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ and the range of $$f^{-1}$$ is $$\left\lbrack {-1,\infty} \right).$$ To find a formula for $$f^{-1},$$ solve the equation $$y = \left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}$$ for $$x.$$ If $$y = \left( {x + 1} \right)^{2},$$ then $$x = -1 \pm \sqrt{y}.$$ Since we are restricting the domain to the interval where $$x \geq -1,$$ we need $$\pm \sqrt{y} \geq 0.$$ Therefore, $$x = -1 + \sqrt{y}.$$ Interchanging $$x$$ and $$y,$$ we write $$y = -1 + \sqrt{x}$$ and conclude that $$f^{-1}(x) = -1 + \sqrt{x}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: The inverse sine function, denoted \sin^{-1} or arcsin, and the inverse cosine function, denoted \cos^{-1} or arccos, are defined on the domain \left. D = \text{\{} x \middle| - 1 \leq x \leq 1 \right\} as follows:...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>The inverse sine function, denoted $$\sin^{-1}$$ or arcsin, and the inverse cosine function, denoted $$\cos^{-1}$$ or arccos, are defined on the domain $$\left. D = \text{\{} x \middle| - 1 \leq x \leq 1 \right\}$$ as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\sin^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \sin (y) = x \text{and} - \frac{\pi}{2} \leq y \leq \frac{\pi}{2};} \\ {\cos^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \cos (y) = x \text{and} 0 \leq y \leq \pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The inverse tangent function, denoted $$\tan^{-1}$$ or arctan, and inverse cotangent function, denoted $$\cot^{-1}$$ or arccot, are defined on the domain $$D = \left\{ x \middle| - \infty < x < \infty \right\}$$ as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\tan^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \tan (y) = x \text{and} - \frac{\pi}{2} < y < \frac{\pi}{2};} \\ {\cot^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \cot (y) = x \text{and} 0 < y < \pi.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The inverse cosecant function, denoted $$\csc^{-1}$$ or arccsc, and inverse secant function, denoted $$\sec^{-1}$$ or arcsec, are defined on the domain $$D = \left\{ x \middle| |x| \geq 1 \right\}$$ as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\csc^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \csc (y) = x \text{and} - \frac{\pi}{2} \leq y \leq \frac{\pi}{2},y \neq 0;} \\ {\sec^{-1}(x) = y \text{if and only if} \sec (y) = x \text{and} 0 \leq y \leq \pi,y \neq \pi/2.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="1.32" title="Evaluating Expressions Involving Inverse Trigonometric Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate each of the following expressions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\sin^{-1}\left( {- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\tan \left( {\tan^{-1}\left( {- \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \right)} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\cos^{-1}\left( {\cos \left( \frac{5\pi}{4} \right)} \right)$$</item>
        <item>$$\sin^{-1}\left( {\cos \left( \frac{2\pi}{3} \right)} \right)$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Evaluating $$\sin^{-1}\left( {-\sqrt{3}/2} \right)$$ is equivalent to finding the angle $$\theta$$ such that $$\sin \theta = -\sqrt{3}/2$$ and $$-\pi/2 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2.$$ The angle $$\theta = -\pi/3$$ satisfies these two conditions. Therefore, $$\sin^{-1}\left( {-\sqrt{3}/2} \right) = -\pi/3.$$</item>
        <item>First we use the fact that $$\tan^{-1}\left( {-1/\sqrt{3}} \right) = -\pi/6.$$ Then $$\tan \left( {{-\pi}/6} \right) = -1/\sqrt{3}.$$ Therefore, $$\tan \left( {\tan^{-1}\left( {-1/\sqrt{3}} \right)} \right) = -1/\sqrt{3}.$$</item>
        <item>To evaluate $$\cos^{-1}\left( {\cos \left( {5\pi/4} \right)} \right),$$ first use the fact that $$\cos \left( {5\pi/4} \right) = -\sqrt{2}/2.$$ Then we need to find the angle $$\theta$$ such that $$\cos (\theta) = -\sqrt{2}/2$$ and $$0 \leq \theta \leq \pi.$$ Since $$3\pi/4$$ satisfies both these conditions, we have $$\cos^{- 1}\left( \cos \left( 5\pi/4 \right) \right) = \cos^{-1}\left( -\sqrt{2}/2 \right) = 3\pi/4.$$</item>
        <item>Since $$\cos \left( {2\pi/3} \right) = -1/2,$$ we need to evaluate $$\sin^{-1}\left( {-1/2} \right).$$ That is, we need to find the angle $$\theta$$ such that $$\sin (\theta) = -1/2$$ and $$-\pi/2 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2.$$ Since $$-\pi/6$$ satisfies both these conditions, we can conclude that $$\sin^{-1}\left( {\cos \left( {2\pi/3} \right)} \right) = \sin^{-1}\left( {-1/2} \right) = -\pi/6.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Bacterial Growth: Suppose a particular population of bacteria is known to double in size every 4 hours. If a culture starts with 1000 bacteria, the number of bacteria after 4 hours is n(4) = 1000 \cdot 2. The number of bacteria after 8...
body_xml:
<example number="1.33" title="Bacterial Growth">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose a particular population of bacteria is known to double in size every $$4$$ hours. If a culture starts with $$1000$$ bacteria, the number of bacteria after $$4$$ hours is $$n(4) = 1000 \cdot 2.$$ The number of bacteria after $$8$$ hours is $$n(8) = n(4) \cdot 2 = 1000 \cdot 2^{2}.$$ In general, the number of bacteria after $$4m$$ hours is $$n(4m) = 1000 \cdot 2^{m}.$$ Letting $$t = 4m,$$ we see that the number of bacteria after $$t$$ hours is $$n(t) = 1000 \cdot 2^{t/4}.$$ Find the number of bacteria after $$6$$ hours, $$10$$ hours, and $$24$$ hours.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The number of bacteria after 6 hours is given by $$n(6) = 1000 \cdot 2^{6/4} \approx 2828$$ bacteria. The number of bacteria after $$10$$ hours is given by $$n(10) = 1000 \cdot 2^{10/4} \approx 5657$$ bacteria. The number of bacteria after $$24$$ hours is given by $$n(24) = 1000 \cdot 2^{6} = 64,000$$ bacteria.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="1.35" title="Compounding Interest">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose $$\$500$$ is invested in an account at an annual interest rate of $$r = 5.5\%,$$ compounded continuously.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$t$$ denote the number of years after the initial investment and $$A(t)$$ denote the amount of money in the account at time $$t.$$ Find a formula for $$A(t).$$</item>
        <item>Find the amount of money in the account after $$10$$ years and after $$20$$ years.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>If $$P$$ dollars are invested in an account at an annual interest rate $$r,$$ compounded continuously, then $$A(t) = Pe^{rt}.$$ Here $$P = \$500$$ and $$r = 0.055.$$ Therefore, $$A(t) = 500e^{0.055t}.$$</item>
        <item>After $$10$$ years, the amount of money in the account is $$A(10) = 500e^{0.055 \cdot 10} = 500e^{0.55} \approx \$866.63.$$ After $$20$$ years, the amount of money in the account is $$A(20) = 500e^{0.055 \cdot 20} = 500e^{1.1} \approx \$1,502.08.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Solving Equations Involving Exponential Functions: Solve each of the following equations for x. 5^{x} = 2 e^{x} + 6e^{-x} = 5 Applying the natural logarithm function to both sides of the equation, we have \ln 5^{x} = \ln 2. Using the power...
body_xml:
<example number="1.36" title="Solving Equations Involving Exponential Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve each of the following equations for $$x.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$5^{x} = 2$$</item>
        <item>$$e^{x} + 6e^{-x} = 5$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Applying the natural logarithm function to both sides of the equation, we have $$\ln 5^{x} = \ln 2.$$ Using the power property of logarithms, $$x\ln 5 = \ln 2.$$ Therefore, $$x = \ln 2/\ln 5.$$</item>
        <item>Multiplying both sides of the equation by $$e^{x},$$ we arrive at the equation $$e^{2x} + 6 = 5e^{x}.$$ Rewriting this equation as $$e^{2x} - 5e^{x} + 6 = 0,$$ we can then rewrite it as a quadratic equation in $$e^{x}:$$ $$\left( e^{x} \right)^{2} - 5\left( e^{x} \right) + 6 = 0.$$ Now we can solve the quadratic equation. Factoring this equation, we obtain $$\left( {e^{x} - 3} \right)\left( {e^{x} - 2} \right) = 0.$$ Therefore, the solutions satisfy $$e^{x} = 3$$ and $$e^{x} = 2.$$ Taking the natural logarithm of both sides gives us the solutions $$x = \ln 3,\ln 2.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="1.37" title="Solving Equations Involving Logarithmic Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Solve each of the following equations for $$x.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\ln \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = 4$$</item>
        <item>$$\log_{10}\sqrt{x} + \log_{10}x = 2$$</item>
        <item>$$\ln \left( {2x} \right) - 3\ln \left( x^{2} \right) = 0$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>By the definition of the natural logarithm function, $$\ln \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = 4 \text{if and only if} e^{4} = \frac{1}{x}.$$ Therefore, the solution is $$x = 1/e^{4}.$$</item>
        <item>Using the product and power properties of logarithmic functions, rewrite the left-hand side of the equation as $$\log_{10}\sqrt{x} + \log_{10}x = \log_{10}x\sqrt{x} = \log_{10}x^{3/2} = \frac{3}{2}\log_{10}x.$$ Therefore, the equation can be rewritten as $$\frac{3}{2}\log_{10}x = 2 \text{or} \log_{10}x = \frac{4}{3}.$$ The solution is $$x = 10^{4/3} = 10\sqrt[3]{10}.$$</item>
        <item>Using the power property of logarithmic functions, we can rewrite the equation as $$\ln \left( {2x} \right) - \ln \left( x^{6} \right) = 0.$$ Using the quotient property, this becomes $$\ln \left( \frac{2}{x^{5}} \right) = 0.$$ Therefore, $$2/x^{5} = 1,$$ which implies $$x = \sqrt[5]{2}.$$ We should then check for any extraneous solutions.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Rule: Change-of-Base Formulas: Let a > 0,b > 0, and a \neq 1,b \neq 1. a^{x} = b^{x\log_{b}a} for any real number x. If b = e, this equation reduces to a^{x} = e^{x\log_{e}a} = e^{x\ln a}. \log_{a}x = \frac{\log_{b}x}{\log_{b}a} for any...

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Change-of-Base Formulas" title="Rule: Change-of-Base Formulas">
    <paragraph>Let $$a > 0,b > 0,$$ and $$a \neq 1,b \neq 1.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$a^{x} = b^{x\log_{b}a}$$ for any real number $$x.$$ If $$b = e,$$ this equation reduces to $$a^{x} = e^{x\log_{e}a} = e^{x\ln a}.$$</item>
      <item>$$\log_{a}x = \frac{\log_{b}x}{\log_{b}a}$$ for any real number $$x > 0.$$ If $$b = e,$$ this equation reduces to $$\log_{a}x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Chapter Opener: The Richter Scale for Earthquakes
snippet: Chapter Opener: The Richter Scale for Earthquakes: In 1935, Charles Richter developed a scale (now known as the Richter scale) to measure the magnitude of an earthquake. The scale is a base-10 logarithmic scale, and it can be described as...
body_xml: In 1935, Charles Richter developed a scale (now known as the Richter scale) to measure the magnitude of an earthquake. The scale is a base-10 logarithmic scale, and it can be described as follows: Consider one earthquake with magnitude $$R_{1}$$ on the Richter scale and a second earthquake with magnitude $$R_{2}$$ on the Richter scale. Suppose $$R_{1} > R_{2},$$ which means the earthquake of magnitude $$R_{1}$$ is stronger, but how much stronger is it than the other earthquake? A way of measuring the intensity of an earthquake is by using a seismograph to measure the amplitude of the earthquake waves. If $$A_{1}$$ is the amplitude measured for the first earthquake and $$A_{2}$$ is the amplitude measured for the second earthquake, then the amplitudes and magnitudes of the two earthquakes satisfy the following equation: $$R_{1} - R_{2} = \log_{10}\left( \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \right).$$ Consider an earthquake that measures 8 on the Richter scale and an earthquake that measures 7 on the Richter scale. Then, $$8 - 7 = \log_{10}\left( \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \right).$$ Therefore, $$\log_{10}\left( \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \right) = 1,$$ which implies $$A_{1}/A_{2} = 10$$ or $$A_{1} = 10A_{2}.$$ Since $$A_{1}$$ is 10 times the size of $$A_{2},$$ we say that the first earthquake is 10 times as intense as the second earthquake. On the other hand, if one earthquake measures 8 on the Richter scale and another measures 6, then the relative intensity of the two earthquakes satisfies the equation $$\log_{10}\left( \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \right) = 8 - 6 = 2.$$ Therefore, $$A_{1} = 100A_{2}.$$ That is, the first earthquake is 100 times more intense than the second earthquake. How can we use logarithmic functions to compare the relative severity of the magnitude 9 earthquake in Japan in 2011 with the magnitude 7.3 earthquake in Haiti in 2010? To compare the Japan and Haiti earthquakes, we can use an equation presented earlier: $$9 - 7.3 = \log_{10}\left( \frac{A_{1}}{A_{2}} \right).$$ Therefore, $$A_{1}/A_{2} = 10^{1.7},$$ and we conclude that the earthquake in Japan was approximately $$50$$ times more intense than the earthquake in Haiti.

title: Evaluating Hyperbolic Functions
snippet: Evaluating Hyperbolic Functions: Simplify \sinh (5\ln x). If \sinh x = 3/4, find the values of the remaining five hyperbolic functions. Using the definition of the \sinh function, we write \sinh (5\ln x) = \frac{e^{5\ln x} - e^{-5\ln...
body_xml:
<example number="1.40" title="Evaluating Hyperbolic Functions">
    <problem>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Simplify $$\sinh (5\ln x).$$</item>
        <item>If $$\sinh x = 3/4,$$ find the values of the remaining five hyperbolic functions.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using the definition of the $$\sinh$$ function, we write $$\sinh (5\ln x) = \frac{e^{5\ln x} - e^{-5\ln x}}{2} = \frac{e^{\ln {(x^{5})}} - e^{\ln {(x^{-5})}}}{2} = \frac{x^{5} - x^{-5}}{2}.$$</item>
        <item>Using the identity $$\cosh^{2}x - \sinh^{2}x = 1,$$ we see that $$\cosh^{2}x = 1 + \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^{2} = \frac{25}{16}.$$ Since $$\cosh x \geq 1$$ for all $$x,$$ we must have $$\cosh x = 5/4.$$ Then, using the definitions for the other hyperbolic functions, we conclude that $$\tanh x = 3/5, \text{csch} x = 4/3, \text{sech} x = 4/5,$$ and $$\coth x = 5/3.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined at all values in an open interval containing a, with the possible exception of a itself, and let L be a real number. If all values of the function $$f(x)$$ approach the real number L as the values of $$x\left( {\neq a} \right)$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit of $$f(x)$$ as x approaches a is L. (More succinct, as x gets closer to a, $$f(x)$$ gets closer and stays close to L.) Symbolically, we express this idea as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Evaluating a Limit Using a Table of Functional Values</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x),$$ we begin by completing a table of functional values. We should choose two sets of x-values—one set of values approaching a and less than a, and another set of values approaching a and greater than a. Table 2.1 demonstrates what your tables might look like. x $$f(x)$$ x $$f(x)$$ $$a - 0.1$$ $$f\left( {a - 0.1} \right)$$ $$a + 0.1$$ $$f\left( {a + 0.1} \right)$$ $$a - 0.01$$ $$f\left( {a - 0.01} \right)$$ $$a + 0.01$$ $$f\left( {a + 0.01} \right)$$ $$a - 0.001$$ $$f\left( {a - 0.001} \right)$$ $$a + 0.001$$ $$f\left( {a + 0.001} \right)$$ $$a - 0.0001$$ $$f\left( {a - 0.0001} \right)$$ $$a + 0.0001$$ $$f\left( {a + 0.0001} \right)$$ Use additional values as necessary. Use additional values as necessary. Table 2.1 Table of Functional Values for $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$</item>
      <item>Next, let’s look at the values in each of the $$f(x)$$ columns and determine whether the values seem to be approaching a single value as we move down each column. In our columns, we look at the sequence $$f\left( {a - 0.1} \right),f\left( {a - 0.01} \right),f\left( {a - 0.001} \right).,f\left( {a - 0.0001} \right),$$ and so on, and $$f\left( {a + 0.1} \right),f\left( {a + 0.01} \right),f\left( {a + 0.001} \right),f\left( {a + 0.0001} \right),$$ and so on. (Note: Although we have chosen the x-values $$a \pm 0.1,a \pm 0.01,a \pm 0.001,a \pm 0.0001,$$ and so forth, and these values will probably work nearly every time, on very rare occasions we may need to modify our choices.)</item>
      <item>If both columns approach a common y-value L, we state $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L.$$ We can use the following strategy to confirm the result obtained from the table or as an alternative method for estimating a limit.</item>
      <item>Using a graphing calculator or computer software that allows us to graph functions, we can plot the function $$f(x),$$ making sure the functional values of $$f(x)$$ for x-values near a are in our window. We can use the trace feature to move along the graph of the function and watch the y-value readout as the x-values approach a. If the y-values approach L as our x-values approach a from both directions, then $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L.$$ We may need to zoom in on our graph and repeat this process several times.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sin \left( {1/\textit{x}} \right)$$ using a table of values. Table 2.5 lists values for the function $$\sin ({1/{x)}}$$ for the given values of x. x $$\sin \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)$$ x $$\sin \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)$$ −0.1 0.544021110889 0.1 −0.544021110889 −0.01 0.50636564111 0.01 −0.50636564111 −0.001 −0.8268795405312 0.001 0.826879540532 −0.0001 0.305614388888 0.0001 −0.305614388888 −0.00001 −0.035748797987 0.00001 0.035748797987 −0.000001 0.349993504187 0.000001 −0.349993504187
After examining the table of functional values, we can see that the y-values do not seem to approach any one single value. It appears the limit does not exist. Before drawing this conclusion, let’s take a more systematic approach. Take the following sequence of x-values approaching 0: $$\frac{2}{\pi},\frac{2}{3\pi},\frac{2}{5\pi},\frac{2}{7\pi},\frac{2}{9\pi},\frac{2}{11\pi} \text{,….}$$ The corresponding y-values are $$1,-1,1,-1,1,-1 \text{,….}$$ At this point we can indeed conclude that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sin \left( {1/\textit{x}} \right)$$ does not exist. (Mathematicians frequently abbreviate “does not exist” as DNE. Thus, we would write $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\sin \left( {1/\textit{x}} \right)$$ DNE.) The graph of $$f(x) = \sin \left( {1/x} \right)$$ is shown in Figure 2.17 and it gives a clearer picture of the behavior of $$\sin ({1/{x)}}$$ as x approaches 0. You can see that $$\sin ({1/{\textit{x})}}$$ oscillates ever more wildly between −1 and 1 as x approaches 0.

title: Definition

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>We define two types of one-sided limits.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Limit from the left: Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined at all values in an open interval of the form (c, a), and let L be a real number. If the values of the function $$f(x)$$ approach the real number L as the values of x (where $$x < \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that L is the limit of $$f(x)$$ as x approaches a from the left. Symbolically, we express this idea as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = L.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Limit from the right: Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined at all values in an open interval of the form $$\left( {a,c} \right),$$ and let L be a real number. If the values of the function $$f(x)$$ approach the real number L as the values of x (where $$x > \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that L is the limit of $$f(x)$$ as x approaches a from the right. Symbolically, we express this idea as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = L.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: We define three types of infinite limits. Infinite limits from the left: Let f(x) be a function defined at all values in an open interval of the form \left( {b,a} \right). If the values of f(x) increase without bound as the...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>We define three types of infinite limits.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Infinite limits from the left: Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined at all values in an open interval of the form $$\left( {b,a} \right).$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ increase without bound as the values of x (where $$x < \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a from the left is positive infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = +\infty.$$ (2.8)</item>
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ decrease without bound as the values of x (where $$x < \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a from the left is negative infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = -\infty.$$ (2.9)</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Infinite limits from the right: Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined at all values in an open interval of the form $$\left( {a,c} \right).$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ increase without bound as the values of x (where $$x > \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a from the right is positive infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = +\infty.$$ (2.10)</item>
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ decrease without bound as the values of x (where $$x > \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a from the right is negative infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = -\infty.$$ (2.11)</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>Two-sided infinite limit: Let $$f(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ in an open interval containing a.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ increase without bound as the values of x (where $$x \neq \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a is positive infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = +\infty.$$ (2.12)</item>
      <item>If the values of $$f(x)$$ decrease without bound as the values of x (where $$x \neq \textit{a})$$ approach the number a, then we say that the limit as x approaches a is negative infinity and we write $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = -\infty.$$ (2.13)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
Evaluate each of the following limits, if possible. Use a table of functional values and graph $$f(x) = {1/x}$$ to confirm your conclusion. $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x}$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x}$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1}{x}$$ Begin by constructing a table of functional values. x $$\frac{1}{x}$$ x $$\frac{1}{x}$$ −0.1 −10 0.1 10 −0.01 −100 0.01 100 −0.001 −1000 0.001 1000 −0.0001 −10,000 0.0001 10,000 −0.00001 −100,000 0.00001 100,000 −0.000001 −1,000,000 0.000001 1,000,000
The values of $$1/x$$ decrease without bound as x approaches 0 from the left. We conclude that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} = -\infty.$$ The values of $$1/x$$ increase without bound as x approaches 0 from the right. We conclude that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} = +\infty.$$ Since $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} = -\infty$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} = +\infty$$ have different values, we conclude that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1}{x} \text{DNE.}$$ The graph of $$f(x) = {1/x}$$ in Figure 2.19 confirms these conclusions.

title: Chapter Opener: Einstein’s Equation
snippet: Chapter Opener: Einstein’s Equation: In the chapter opener we mentioned briefly how Albert Einstein showed that a limit exists to how fast any object can travel. Given Einstein’s equation for the mass of a moving object, what is the value...
body_xml:
In the chapter opener we mentioned briefly how Albert Einstein showed that a limit exists to how fast any object can travel. Given Einstein’s equation for the mass of a moving object, what is the value of this bound? Our starting point is Einstein’s equation for the mass of a moving object, $$m = \frac{m_{0}}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}},$$ where $$m_{0}$$ is the object’s mass at rest, v is its speed, and c is the speed of light. To see how the mass changes at high speeds, we can graph the ratio of masses $$m/m_{0}$$ as a function of the ratio of speeds, $$v/c$$ (Figure 2.23). We can see that as the ratio of speeds approaches 1—that is, as the speed of the object approaches the speed of light—the ratio of masses increases without bound. In other words, the function has a vertical asymptote at $${v/c} = 1.$$ We can try a few values of this ratio to test this idea. $$\frac{v}{c}$$ $$\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}$$ $$\frac{m}{m_{0}}$$ 0.99 0.1411 7.089 0.999 0.0447 22.37 0.9999 0.0141 70.71
Thus, according to Table 2.8, if an object with mass 100 kg is traveling at 0.9999c, its mass becomes 7071 kg. Since no object can have an infinite mass, we conclude that no object can travel at or more than the speed of light.

    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The limit of x as x approaches a is a: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x = 2.$$</item>
        <item>The limit of a constant is that constant: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }5 = 5.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Limit Laws
snippet: Limit Laws: Limit Laws Let f(x) and g(x) be defined for all x \neq a over some open interval containing a. Assume that L and M are real numbers such that \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L and \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) =...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="2.5" title="Limit Laws">
    <heading level="4">Limit Laws</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ over some open interval containing a. Assume that L and M are real numbers such that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = M.$$ Let c be a constant. Then, each of the following statements holds:</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Sum law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) + g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) + \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L + M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Difference law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) - g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) - \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L - M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Constant multiple law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }cf(x) = c \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = cL$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Product law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x) \cdot g(x)} \right) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x) = L \cdot M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Quotient law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)}{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}$$ for $$M \neq 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Power law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\left( {f(x)} \right)^{n} = \left( {\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)} \right)^{n} = L^{n}$$ for every positive integer n.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Root law for limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\sqrt[n]{f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{L}$$ for all L if n is odd and for $$L \geq 0$$ if n is even and $$f(x) \geq 0$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Evaluating a Limit Using Limit Laws
snippet: Evaluating a Limit Using Limit Laws: Use the limit laws to evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2} \right). Let’s apply the limit laws one step at a time to be sure we understand how they work. We need to keep in mind the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.14" title="Evaluating a Limit Using Limit Laws">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the limit laws to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let’s apply the limit laws one step at a time to be sure we understand how they work. We need to keep in mind the requirement that, at each application of a limit law, the new limits must exist for the limit law to be applied.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{clccl} {\underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2} \right)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }4x + \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }2} & & & \text{Apply the sum law.} \\ & {= 4 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow-3}{\lim }2} & & & \text{Apply the constant multiple law.} \\ & {= 4 \cdot (-3) + 2 = -10.} & & & \text{Apply the basic limit results and simplify.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Limit Laws Repeatedly
snippet: Using Limit Laws Repeatedly: Use the limit laws to evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 3x + 1}{x^{3} + 4}. To find this limit, we need to apply the limit laws several times. Again, we need to keep in mind that as we...
body_xml:
<example number="2.15" title="Using Limit Laws Repeatedly">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the limit laws to evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 3x + 1}{x^{3} + 4}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find this limit, we need to apply the limit laws several times. Again, we need to keep in mind that as we rewrite the limit in terms of other limits, each new limit must exist for the limit law to be applied.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$\begin{array}{clccl} & & & & \\ & & & & \\ {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{2x^{2} - 3x + 1}{x^{3} + 4}} & {= \frac{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\left( {2x^{2} - 3x + 1} \right)}{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\left( {x^{3} + 4} \right)}} & & & { \text{Apply the quotient law, making sure that.} (2)^{3} + 4 \neq 0} \\ & {= \frac{2 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{2} - 3 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }1}{\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{3} + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }4}} & & & \text{Apply the sum law and constant multiple law.} \\ & {= \frac{2 \cdot \left( {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x} \right)^{2} - 3 \cdot \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }1}{\left( {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x} \right)^{3} + \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }4}} & & & \text{Apply the power law.} \\ & {= \frac{2(4) - 3(2) + 1}{(2)^{3} + 4} = \frac{1}{4}.} & & & \text{Apply the basic limit laws and simplify.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Calculating a Limit When $$f(x)/g(x)$$ has the Indeterminate Form 0/0</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>First, we need to make sure that our function has the appropriate form and cannot be evaluated immediately using the limit laws.</item>
      <item>We then need to find a function that is equal to $$h(x) = {{f(x)}/{g(x)}}$$ for all $$x \neq a$$ over some interval containing a. To do this, we may need to try one or more of the following steps: If $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ are polynomials, we should factor each function and cancel out any common factors. If the numerator or denominator contains a difference involving a square root, we should try multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the expression involving the square root. If $${f(x)}/{g(x)}$$ is a complex fraction, we begin by simplifying it.</item>
      <item>Last, we apply the limit laws.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Evaluating a Limit by Factoring and Canceling
snippet: Evaluating a Limit by Factoring and Canceling: Evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3}. Step 1. The function f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3} is undefined for x = 3. In fact, if we substitute 3...
body_xml:
<example number="2.17" title="Evaluating a Limit by Factoring and Canceling">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. The function $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3}$$ is undefined for $$x = 3.$$ In fact, if we substitute 3 into the function we get $${0/0},$$ which is indeterminate. Factoring and canceling is a good strategy:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3} = \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x\left( {x - 3} \right)}{\left( {x - 3} \right)\left( {2x + 1} \right)}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. For all $$x \neq 3,\frac{x^{2} - 3x}{2x^{2} - 5x - 3} = \frac{x}{2x + 1}.$$ Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x\left( {x - 3} \right)}{\left( {x - 3} \right)\left( {2x + 1} \right)} = \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x}{2x + 1}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. Evaluate using the limit laws:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x}{2x + 1} = \frac{3}{7}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating a Limit by Multiplying by a Conjugate
snippet: Evaluating a Limit by Multiplying by a Conjugate: Evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1}. Step 1. \frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1} has the form 0/0 at −1. Let’s begin by multiplying by \sqrt{x + 2} + 1, the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.18" title="Evaluating a Limit by Multiplying by a Conjugate">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. $$\frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1}$$ has the form $$0/0$$ at −1. Let’s begin by multiplying by $$\sqrt{x + 2} + 1,$$ the conjugate of $$\sqrt{x + 2} - 1,$$ on the numerator and denominator:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1} = \underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + 2} - 1}{x + 1} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x + 2} + 1}{\sqrt{x + 2} + 1}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. We then multiply out the numerator. We don’t multiply out the denominator because we are hoping that the $$\left( {x + 1} \right)$$ in the denominator cancels out in the end:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{x + 1}{\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {\sqrt{x + 2} + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. Then we cancel:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 2} + 1}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4. Last, we apply the limit laws:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 2} + 1} = \frac{1}{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating a Limit by Simplifying a Complex Fraction
snippet: Evaluating a Limit by Simplifying a Complex Fraction: Evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1}. Step 1. \frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1} has the form 0/0 at 1. We simplify the...
body_xml:
<example number="2.19" title="Evaluating a Limit by Simplifying a Complex Fraction">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. $$\frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1}$$ has the form $$0/0$$ at 1. We simplify the algebraic fraction by multiplying by $${{2\left( {x + 1} \right)}/{2\left( {x + 1} \right)}}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1} = \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 1} \cdot \frac{2\left( {x + 1} \right)}{2\left( {x + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. Next, we multiply through the numerators. Do not multiply the denominators because we want to be able to cancel the factor $$\left( {x - 1} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{2 - \left( {x + 1} \right)}{2\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. Then, we simplify the numerator:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{- x + 1}{2\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 4. Now we factor out −1 from the numerator:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{- \left( {x - 1} \right)}{2\left( {x - 1} \right)\left( {x + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 5. Then, we cancel the common factors of $$\left( {x - 1} \right):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{-1}{2\left( {x + 1} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 6. Last, we evaluate using the limit laws:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\frac{-1}{2(x + 1)} = - \frac{1}{4}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating a Limit When the Limit Laws Do Not Apply
snippet: Evaluating a Limit When the Limit Laws Do Not Apply: Evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {\frac{1}{x} + \frac{5}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} \right). Both 1/x and 5/{x\left( {x - 5} \right)} fail to have a limit at zero. Since...
body_xml:
<example number="2.20" title="Evaluating a Limit When the Limit Laws Do Not Apply">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {\frac{1}{x} + \frac{5}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Both $$1/x$$ and $$5/{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}$$ fail to have a limit at zero. Since neither of the two functions has a limit at zero, we cannot apply the sum law for limits; we must use a different strategy. In this case, we find the limit by performing addition and then applying one of our previous strategies. Observe that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{1}{x} + \frac{5}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} & {= \frac{x - 5 + 5}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} \\ & {= \frac{x}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {\frac{1}{x} + \frac{5}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} \right)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{x}{x\left( {x - 5} \right)}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1}{x - 5}} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{5}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
