title: Evaluating a One-Sided Limit Using the Limit Laws
snippet: Evaluating a One-Sided Limit Using the Limit Laws: Evaluate each of the following limits, if possible. \underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3} \underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3} Figure 2.25 illustrates the function...
body_xml: Evaluate each of the following limits, if possible. $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$ Figure 2.25 illustrates the function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ and aids in our understanding of these limits. The function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is defined over the interval $$\left\lbrack {3,+\infty} \right).$$ Since this function is not defined to the left of 3, we cannot apply the limit laws to compute $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}.$$ In fact, since $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is undefined to the left of 3, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}$$ does not exist. Since $$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 3}$$ is defined to the right of 3, the limit laws do apply to $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3}.$$ By applying these limit laws we obtain $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 3} = 0.$$

title: Evaluating a Two-Sided Limit Using the Limit Laws
snippet: Evaluating a Two-Sided Limit Using the Limit Laws: For f(x) = \begin{cases} {4x - 3} & { \text{if} x < 2} \\ \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} & { \text{if} x \geq 2} \end{cases}, evaluate each of the following limits: \underset{x\rightarrow...
body_xml: For $$f(x) = \begin{cases} {4x - 3} & { \text{if} x < 2} \\ \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} & { \text{if} x \geq 2} \end{cases},$$ evaluate each of the following limits: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }f(x)$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}{\lim }f(x)$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }f(x)$$ Figure 2.26 illustrates the function $$f(x)$$ and aids in our understanding of these limits. Since $$f(x) = 4x - 3$$ for all x in $$\left( {-\infty,2} \right),$$ replace $$f(x)$$ in the limit with $$4x - 3$$ and apply the limit laws: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = \underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\left( {4x - 3} \right) = 5.$$ Since $$f(x) = \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}$$ for all x in $$\left( {2,+\infty} \right),$$ replace $$f(x)$$ in the limit with $$\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}$$ and apply the limit laws: $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = \underset{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}{\lim }\left( {x - 3} \right)^{2} = 1.$$ Since $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = 5$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = 1,$$ we conclude that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }f(x)$$ does not exist.

title: Evaluating a Limit of the Form K/0,K≠0K/0,K≠0 Using the Limit Laws
snippet: Evaluating a Limit of the Form K/0,K≠0K/0,K≠0 Using the Limit Laws: Evaluate \underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x^{2} - 2x}. Step 1. After substituting in x = 2, we see that this limit has the form -1/0. That is, as x...
body_xml:
<example number="2.23" title="Evaluating a Limit of the Form K/0,K≠0K/0,K≠0 Using the Limit Laws">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x^{2} - 2x}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Step 1. After substituting in $$x = 2,$$ we see that this limit has the form $$-1/0.$$ That is, as x approaches 2 from the left, the numerator approaches −1; and the denominator approaches 0. Consequently, the magnitude of $$\frac{x - 3}{x(x - 2)}$$ becomes infinite. To get a better idea of what the limit is, we need to factor the denominator:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x^{2} - 2x} = \underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x\left( {x - 2} \right)}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 2. Since $$x - 2$$ is the only part of the denominator that is zero when 2 is substituted, we then separate $${1/{(x - 2}})$$ from the rest of the function:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= \underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x} \cdot \frac{1}{x - 2}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Step 3. $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x} = - \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{1}{x - 2} = -\infty.$$ Therefore, the product of $${(x - 3)}/x$$ and $${1/{(x - 2}})$$ has a limit of $$\text{+∞:}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow 2^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x - 3}{x^{2} - 2x} = +\infty.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating an Important Trigonometric Limit
snippet: Evaluating an Important Trigonometric Limit: Evaluate \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta}. In the first step, we multiply by the conjugate so that we can use a trigonometric identity to convert the cosine in...
body_xml:
<example number="2.25" title="Evaluating an Important Trigonometric Limit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate $$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>In the first step, we multiply by the conjugate so that we can use a trigonometric identity to convert the cosine in the numerator to a sine:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta}} & {= \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta} \cdot \frac{1 + \cos \theta}{1 + \cos \theta}} \\ & {= \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos^{2}\theta}{\theta\left( {1 + \cos \theta} \right)}} \\ & {= \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\theta\left( {1 + \cos \theta} \right)}} \\ & {= \underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin \theta}{\theta} \cdot \frac{\sin \theta}{1 + \cos \theta}} \\ & {= 1 \cdot \frac{0}{2} = 0.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{\theta\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1 - \cos \theta}{\theta} = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph>A function $$f(x)$$ is continuous at a point a if and only if the following three conditions are satisfied:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">

      <item>$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ exists</item>

<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Determining Continuity at a Point</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Check to see if $$f(a)$$ is defined. If $$f(a)$$ is undefined, we need go no further. The function is not continuous at a. If $$f(a)$$ is defined, continue to step 2.</item>
      <item>Compute $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x).$$ In some cases, we may need to do this by first computing $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x).$$ If $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ does not exist (that is, it is not a real number), then the function is not continuous at a and the problem is solved. If $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ exists, then continue to step 3.</item>
      <item>Compare $$f(a)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x).$$ If $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) \neq f(a),$$ then the function is not continuous at a. If $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = f(a),$$ then the function is continuous at a.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

Let’s begin by trying to calculate $$f(3).$$ $$f(3) = - {(3^{2})} + 4 = -5.$$ Thus, $$f(3)$$ is defined. Next, we calculate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }f(x).$$ To do this, we must compute $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }f(x)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }f(x):$$ $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = - {(3^{2})} + 4 = -5$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = 4(3) - 8 = 4.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }f(x)$$ does not exist. snippet: Definition: If f(x) is discontinuous at a, then f has a removable discontinuity at a if \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) exists. (Note: When we state that \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) exists, we mean that \underset{x\rightarrow...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>If $$f(x)$$ is discontinuous at a, then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f$$ has a removable discontinuity at a if $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ exists. (Note: When we state that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x)$$ exists, we mean that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L,$$ where L is a real number.)</item>
      <item>$$f$$ has a jump discontinuity at a if $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x)$$ both exist, but $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) \neq \underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x).$$ (Note: When we state that $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x)$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x)$$ both exist, we mean that both are real-valued and that neither take on the values ±∞.)</item>
      <item>$$f$$ has an infinite discontinuity at a if $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = \text{±} \infty$$ and/or $$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = \text{±} \infty.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Classifying a Discontinuity
snippet: Classifying a Discontinuity: In Example 2.26, we showed that f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2} is discontinuous at x = 2. Classify this discontinuity as removable, jump, or infinite. To classify the discontinuity at 2 we must evaluate...
body_xml:
<example number="2.30" title="Classifying a Discontinuity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>In Example 2.26, we showed that $$f(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2}$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2.$$ Classify this discontinuity as removable, jump, or infinite.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To classify the discontinuity at 2 we must evaluate $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }f(x):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }f(x)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 2} \right)}{x - 2}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\left( {x + 2} \right)} \\ & {= 4.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since f is discontinuous at 2 and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }f(x)$$ exists, f has a removable discontinuity at $$x = 2.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Earlier, we showed that f is discontinuous at 3 because $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }f(x)$$ does not exist. However, since $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = -5$$ and $$\underset{x\rightarrow 3^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = 4$$ both exist, we conclude that the function has a jump discontinuity at 3.</paragraph>
    </solution>

      <paragraph>Since $$f(x) = x - \cos x$$ is continuous over $$\left( {-\infty,+\infty} \right),$$ it is continuous over any closed interval of the form $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$ If you can find an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ such that $$f(a)$$ and $$f(b)$$ have opposite signs, you can use the Intermediate Value Theorem to conclude there must be a real number c in $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ that satisfies $$f(c) = 0.$$ Note that</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(0) = 0 - \cos (0) = -1 < 0$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \cos \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2} > 0.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the Intermediate Value Theorem, we can see that there must be a real number c in $$\left\lbrack {0,{\pi/2}} \right\rbrack$$ that satisfies $$f(c) = 0.$$ Therefore, $$f(x) = x - \cos x$$ has at least one zero.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: When Can You Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem?
snippet: When Can You Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem?: If f(x) is continuous over \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack,f(0) > 0 and f(2) > 0, can we use the Intermediate Value Theorem to conclude that f(x) has no zeros in the interval...
body_xml:
<example number="2.37" title="When Can You Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem?">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If $$f(x)$$ is continuous over $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack,f(0) > 0$$ and $$f(2) > 0,$$ can we use the Intermediate Value Theorem to conclude that $$f(x)$$ has no zeros in the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \text{]?} \right.$$ Explain.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>No. The Intermediate Value Theorem only allows us to conclude that we can find a value between $$f(0)$$ and $$f(2);$$ it doesn’t allow us to conclude that we can’t find other values. To see this more clearly, consider the function $$f(x) = \left( {x - 1} \right)^{2}.$$ It satisfies $$f(0) = 1 > 0,f(2) = 1 > 0,$$ and $$f(1) = 0.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ over an open interval containing a. Let L be a real number. Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if, for every $$\varepsilon > 0,$$ there exists a $$\delta > 0,$$ such that if $$\left. 0 < \middle| x - a \middle| < \delta, \right.$$ then $$\left| f(x) - L \middle| < \varepsilon. \right.$$</paragraph>

title: Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function
snippet: Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function: Prove that \underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\left( {2x + 1} \right) = 3. Let \varepsilon > 0. The first part of the definition begins “For every \varepsilon > 0 \text{.”} This...
body_xml: Prove that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\left( {2x + 1} \right) = 3.$$ Let $$\varepsilon > 0.$$ The first part of the definition begins “For every $$\varepsilon > 0 \text{.”}$$ This means we must prove that whatever follows is true no matter what positive value of ε is chosen. By stating “Let $$\varepsilon > 0 \text{,”}$$ we signal our intent to do so. Choose $$\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.$$ The definition continues with “there exists a $$\delta > 0.$$ ” The phrase “there exists” in a mathematical statement is always a signal for a scavenger hunt. In other words, we must go and find $$\delta.$$ So, where exactly did $$\delta = {\varepsilon/2}$$ come from? There are two basic approaches to tracking down $$\delta.$$ One method is purely algebraic and the other is geometric. We begin by tackling the problem from an algebraic point of view. Since ultimately we want $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| < \varepsilon,$$ we begin by manipulating this expression: $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| < \varepsilon$$ is equivalent to $$\left| {2x - 2} \right| < \varepsilon,$$ which in turn is equivalent to $$|2|\left| {x - 1} \right| < \varepsilon.$$ Last, this is equivalent to $$\left| {x - 1} \right| < {\varepsilon/2}.$$ Thus, it would seem that $$\delta = {\varepsilon/2}$$ is appropriate. We may also find $$\delta$$ through geometric methods. Figure 2.40 demonstrates how this is done. Assume $$0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta.$$ When $$\delta$$ has been chosen, our goal is to show that if $$0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta,$$ then $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| < \varepsilon.$$ To prove any statement of the form “If this, then that,” we begin by assuming “this” and trying to get “that.” Thus, $$\begin{array}{clccc} \left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| & {= \left| {2x - 2} \right|} & & & \text{property of absolute value} \\ & {= \left| {2\left( {x - 1} \right)} \right|} & & & \\ & {= |2|\left| {x - 1} \right|} & & & \left| 2 \middle| = 2 \right. \\ & {= 2\left| {x - 1} \right|} & & & \\ & {< 2 \cdot \delta} & & & { \text{here’s where we use the assumption that} 0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta} \\ & {= 2 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon} & & & { \text{here’s where we use our choice of} \delta = {\varepsilon/2}} \end{array}$$ In this part of the proof, we started with $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right|$$ and used our assumption $$0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta$$ in a key part of the chain of inequalities to get $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right|$$ to be less than ε. We could just as easily have manipulated the assumed inequality $$0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta$$ to arrive at $$\left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| < \varepsilon$$ as follows: $$\begin{array}{ll} {0 < |x - 1| < \delta} & {\Rightarrow|x - 1| < \delta} \\ & {\Rightarrow - \delta < x - 1 < \delta} \\ & {\Rightarrow - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < x - 1 < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}} \\ & {\Rightarrow - \varepsilon < 2x - 2 < \varepsilon} \\ & {\Rightarrow|2x - 2| < \varepsilon} \\ & {\Rightarrow\left| (2x + 1) - 3 \right| < \varepsilon.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\left( {2x + 1} \right) = 3.$$ (Having completed the proof, we state what we have accomplished.) After removing all the remarks, here is a final version of the proof: Let $$\varepsilon > 0.$$ Choose $$\delta = {\varepsilon/2}.$$ Assume $$0 < \left| {x - 1} \right| < \delta.$$ Thus, $$\begin{array}{cl} \left| {\left( {2x + 1} \right) - 3} \right| & {= \left| {2x - 2} \right|} \\ & {= \left| {2\left( {x - 1} \right)} \right|} \\ & {= |2|\left| {x - 1} \right|} \\ & {= 2\left| {x - 1} \right|} \\ & {< 2 \cdot \delta} \\ & {= 2 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2}} \\ & {= \varepsilon.} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 1}{\lim }\left( {2x + 1} \right) = 3.$$

snippet: Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function (Geometric Approach): Prove that \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{2} = 4. Let \varepsilon > 0. The first part of the definition begins “For every \varepsilon > 0 \text{,”} so we...
body_xml:
<example number="2.41" title="Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function (Geometric Approach)">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Prove that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{2} = 4.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$\varepsilon > 0.$$ The first part of the definition begins “For every $$\varepsilon > 0 \text{,”}$$ so we must prove that whatever follows is true no matter what positive value of ε is chosen. By stating “Let $$\varepsilon > 0 \text{,”}$$ we signal our intent to do so.</item>
        <item>Without loss of generality, assume $$\varepsilon \leq 4.$$ Two questions present themselves: Why do we want $$\varepsilon \leq 4$$ and why is it okay to make this assumption? In answer to the first question: Later on, in the process of solving for $$\delta,$$ we will discover that $$\delta$$ involves the quantity $$\sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}.$$ Consequently, we need $$\varepsilon \leq 4.$$ In answer to the second question: If we can find $$\delta > 0$$ that “works” for $$\varepsilon \leq 4,$$ then it will “work” for any $$\varepsilon > 4$$ as well. Keep in mind that, although it is always okay to put an upper bound on ε, it is never okay to put a lower bound (other than zero) on ε.</item>
        <item>Choose $$\delta = \min \left\{ {2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon},\sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2} \right\}.$$ Figure 2.41 shows how we made this choice of $$\delta.$$ Figure 2.41 This graph shows how we find δ geometrically for a given ε for the proof in Example 2.41.</item>
        <item>We must show: If $$0 < \left| {x - 2} \right| < \delta,$$ then $${|{x^{2} - 4}|} < \varepsilon,$$ so we must begin by assuming $$0 < \left| {x - 2} \right| < \delta.$$ We don’t really need $$0 < \left| {x - 2} \right|$$ (in other words, $$\left. x \neq 2 \right)$$ for this proof. Since $$0 < \left| {x - 2} \right| < \delta\Rightarrow\left| {x - 2} \right| < \delta,$$ it is okay to drop $$0 < \left| {x - 2} \right|.$$ $$\left| {x - 2} \right| < \delta.$$ Hence, $$- \delta < x - 2 < \delta.$$ Recall that $$\delta = \min \left\{ {2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon},\sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2} \right\}.$$ Thus, $$\delta \leq 2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}$$ and consequently $$- \left( {2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}} \right) \leq - \delta.$$ We also use $$\delta \leq \sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2$$ here. We might ask at this point: Why did we substitute $$2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}$$ for $$\delta$$ on the left-hand side of the inequality and $$\sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2$$ on the right-hand side of the inequality? If we look at Figure 2.41, we see that $$2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}$$ corresponds to the distance on the left of 2 on the x-axis and $$\sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2$$ corresponds to the distance on the right. Thus, $$- \left( {2 - \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon}} \right) \leq - \delta < x - 2 < \delta \leq \sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2.$$ We simplify the expression on the left: $$-2 + \sqrt{4 - \varepsilon} < x - 2 < \sqrt{4 + \varepsilon} - 2.$$ Then, we add 2 to all parts of the inequality: $$\sqrt{4 - \varepsilon} < x < \sqrt{4 + \varepsilon}.$$ We square all parts of the inequality. It is okay to do so, since all parts of the inequality are positive: $$4 - \varepsilon < x^{2} < 4 + \varepsilon.$$ We subtract 4 from all parts of the inequality: $$- \varepsilon < x^{2} - 4 < \varepsilon.$$ Last, $${|{x^{2} - 4}|} < \varepsilon.$$</item>
        <item>Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }x^{2} = 4.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function (Algebraic Approach): Prove that \underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 3} \right) = 6. Let’s use our outline from the Problem-Solving Strategy: Let \varepsilon > 0....
body_xml:
<example number="2.42" title="Proving a Statement about the Limit of a Specific Function (Algebraic Approach)">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Prove that $$\underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 3} \right) = 6.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let’s use our outline from the Problem-Solving Strategy:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Let $$\varepsilon > 0.$$</item>
        <item>Choose $$\delta = \min \left\{ {1,{\varepsilon/5}} \right\}.$$ This choice of $$\delta$$ may appear odd at first glance, but it was obtained by taking a look at our ultimate desired inequality: $$\left| {\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 3} \right) - 6} \right| < \varepsilon.$$ This inequality is equivalent to $$\left| {x + 1} \right| \cdot \left| {x - 3} \right| < \varepsilon.$$ At this point, the temptation simply to choose $$\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{x - 3}$$ is very strong. Unfortunately, our choice of $$\delta$$ must depend on ε only and no other variable. If we can replace $$\left| {x - 3} \right|$$ by a numerical value, our problem can be resolved. This is the place where assuming $$\delta \leq 1$$ comes into play. The choice of $$\delta \leq 1$$ here is arbitrary. We could have just as easily used any other positive number. In some proofs, greater care in this choice may be necessary. Now, since $$\delta \leq 1$$ and $$\left| {x + 1} \right| < \delta \leq 1,$$ we are able to show that $$\left| {x - 3} \right| < 5.$$ Consequently, $$\left| {x + 1} \right| \cdot \left| {x - 3} \right| < \left| {x + 1} \right| \cdot 5.$$ At this point we realize that we also need $$\delta \leq {\varepsilon/5}.$$ Thus, we choose $$\delta = \min \left\{ {1,{\varepsilon/5}} \right\}.$$</item>
        <item>Assume $$0 < \left| {x + 1} \right| < \delta.$$ Thus, $$\left| {x + 1} \right| < 1 \text{and} {\left| {x + 1} \right| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5}.}$$ Since $$\left| {x + 1} \right| < 1,$$ we may conclude that $$-1 < x + 1 < 1.$$ Thus, by subtracting 4 from all parts of the inequality, we obtain $$-5 < x - 3 < -1.$$ Consequently, $$\left| {x - 3} \right| < 5.$$ This gives us $$\left| {\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 3} \right) - 6} \right| = \left| {x + 1} \right| \cdot \left| {x - 3} \right| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5} \cdot 5 = \varepsilon.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow-1}{\lim }\left( {x^{2} - 2x + 3} \right) = 6.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Showing That a Limit Does Not Exist: Show that \underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{|x|}{x} does not exist. The graph of f(x) = {|x|/x} is shown here: Suppose that L is a candidate for a limit. Choose \varepsilon = {1/{2.}} Let \delta >...
body_xml:
<example number="2.43" title="Showing That a Limit Does Not Exist">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Show that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{|x|}{x}$$ does not exist. The graph of $$f(x) = {|x|/x}$$ is shown here:</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Suppose that L is a candidate for a limit. Choose $$\varepsilon = {1/{2.}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$\delta > 0.$$ Either $$L \geq 0$$ or $$L < 0.$$ If $$L \geq 0,$$ then let $$x = - {\delta/2}.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {x - 0} \right| = \left| {- \frac{\delta}{2} - 0} \right| = \frac{\delta}{2} < \delta$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {\frac{\left| {- \frac{\delta}{2}} \right|}{- \frac{\delta}{2}} - L} \right| = \left| {-1 - L} \right| = L + 1 \geq 1 > \frac{1}{2} = \varepsilon.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>On the other hand, if $$L < 0,$$ then let $$x = {\delta/2}.$$ Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {x - 0} \right| = \left| {\frac{\delta}{2} - 0} \right| = \frac{\delta}{2} < \delta$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>and</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left| {\frac{\left| \frac{\delta}{2} \right|}{\frac{\delta}{2}} - L} \right| = \left| {1 - L} \right| = |L| + 1 \geq 1 > \frac{1}{2} = \varepsilon.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, for any value of L, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{|x|}{x} \neq L.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Definition: Limit from the Right: Let f(x) be defined over an open interval of the form \left( {a,b} \right) where a < b. Then, \underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = L if for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists a \delta > 0 such that...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Limit from the Right: Let $$f(x)$$ be defined over an open interval of the form $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ where $$a < b.$$ Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{+}}{\lim }f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every $$\varepsilon > 0,$$ there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that if $$0 < x - a < \delta,$$ then $$\left| {f(x) - L} \right| < \varepsilon.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Limit from the Left: Let $$f(x)$$ be defined over an open interval of the form $$\left( {b,a} \right)$$ where $$b < a.$$ Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every $$\varepsilon > 0,$$ there exists a $$\delta > 0$$ such that if $$- \delta < x - a < 0,$$ then $$\left| {f(x) - L} \right| < \varepsilon.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Proving a Statement about a Limit From the Right
snippet: Proving a Statement about a Limit From the Right: Prove that \underset{x\rightarrow 4^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 4} = 0. Let \varepsilon > 0. Choose \delta = \varepsilon^{2}. Since we ultimately want \left| {\sqrt{x - 4} - 0} \right| <...
body_xml: Prove that $$\underset{x\rightarrow 4^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 4} = 0.$$ Let $$\varepsilon > 0.$$ Choose $$\delta = \varepsilon^{2}.$$ Since we ultimately want $$\left| {\sqrt{x - 4} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon,$$ we manipulate this inequality to get $$\sqrt{x - 4} < \varepsilon$$ or, equivalently, $$0 < x - 4 < \varepsilon^{2},$$ making $$\delta = \varepsilon^{2}$$ a clear choice. We may also determine $$\delta$$ geometrically, as shown in Figure 2.42. Assume $$0 < x - 4 < \delta.$$ Thus, $$0 < x - 4 < \varepsilon^{2}.$$ Hence, $$0 < \sqrt{x - 4} < \varepsilon.$$ Finally, $$\left| {\sqrt{x - 4} - 0} \right| < \varepsilon.$$ Therefore, $$\underset{x\rightarrow 4^{+}}{\lim }\sqrt{x - 4} = 0.$$

snippet: Definition: Let f(x) be defined for all x \neq a in an open interval containing a. Then, we have an infinite limit \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = +\infty if for every M > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that if 0 < \left| {x - a}...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ in an open interval containing a. Then, we have an infinite limit</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = +\infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every $$M > 0,$$ there exists $$\delta > 0$$ such that if $$0 < \left| {x - a} \right| < \delta,$$ then $$f(x) > M.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be defined for all $$x \neq a$$ in an open interval containing a. Then, we have a negative infinite limit</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }f(x) = -\infty$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>if for every $$M > 0,$$ there exists $$\delta > 0$$ such that if $$0 < \left| {x - a} \right| < \delta,$$ then $$f(x) < -M.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function defined on an interval $$I$$ containing $$a.$$ If $$x \neq a$$ is in $$I,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$Q = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is a difference quotient.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Also, if $$h \neq 0$$ is chosen so that $$a + h$$ is in $$I,$$ then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$Q = \frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is a difference quotient with increment $$h.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Definition: Let f(x) be a function defined in an open interval containing a. The tangent line to f(x) at a is the line passing through the point \left( {a,f(a)} \right) having slope m_{\tan } = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x) -...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined in an open interval containing $$a.$$ The tangent line to $$f(x)$$ at $$a$$ is the line passing through the point $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ having slope</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$m_{\tan } = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided this limit exists.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Equivalently, we may define the tangent line to $$f(x)$$ at $$a$$ to be the line passing through the point $$\left( {a,f(a)} \right)$$ having slope</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$m_{\tan } = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided this limit exists.</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding a Tangent Line
snippet: Finding a Tangent Line: Find an equation of the line tangent to the graph of f(x) = x^{2} at x = 3. First find the slope of the tangent line. In this example, use Equation 3.3. \begin{array}{clccl} m_{\tan } & {= \underset{x\rightarrow...
body_xml: Find an equation of the line tangent to the graph of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ at $$x = 3.$$ First find the slope of the tangent line. In this example, use Equation 3.3. $$\begin{array}{clccl} m_{\tan } & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(3)}{x - 3}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 9}{x - 3}} & & & { \text{Substitute} f(x) = x^{2} \text{and} f(3) = 9.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{\left( {x - 3} \right)\left( {x + 3} \right)}{x - 3} = \underset{x\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\left( {x + 3} \right) = 6} & & & \text{Factor the numerator to evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$ Next, find a point on the tangent line. Since the line is tangent to the graph of $$f(x)$$ at $$x = 3,$$ it passes through the point $$\left( {3,f(3)} \right).$$ We have $$f(3) = 9,$$ so the tangent line passes through the point $$\left( {3,9} \right).$$ Using the point-slope equation of the line with the slope $$m = 6$$ and the point $$\left( {3,9} \right),$$ we obtain the line $$y - 9 = 6\left( {x - 3} \right).$$ Simplifying, we have $$y = 6x - 9.$$ The graph of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ and its tangent line at $$3$$ are shown in Figure 3.6.

title: The Slope of a Tangent Line Revisited
snippet: The Slope of a Tangent Line Revisited: Use Equation 3.4 to find the slope of the line tangent to the graph of f(x) = x^{2} at x = 3. The steps are very similar to Example 3.1. See Equation 3.4 for the definition. \begin{array}{clccl}...
body_xml:
<example number="3.2" title="The Slope of a Tangent Line Revisited">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use Equation 3.4 to find the slope of the line tangent to the graph of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ at $$x = 3.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The steps are very similar to Example 3.1. See Equation 3.4 for the definition.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} m_{\tan } & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {3 + h} \right) - f(3)}{h}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {3 + h} \right)^{2} - 9}{h}} & & & { \text{Substitute} f\left( {3 + h} \right) = {(3 + h)}^{2} \text{and} f(3) = 9.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{9 + 6h + h^{2} - 9}{h}} & & & \text{Expand and simplify to evaluate the limit.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h\left( {6 + h} \right)}{h} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {6 + h} \right) = 6} & & & \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We obtained the same value for the slope of the tangent line by using the other definition, demonstrating that the formulas can be interchanged.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line
snippet: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line: Find an equation of the line tangent to the graph of f(x) = 1/x at x = 2. We can use Equation 3.3, but as we have seen, the results are the same if we use Equation 3.4. \begin{array}{clccl} m_{\tan }...
body_xml: Find an equation of the line tangent to the graph of $$f(x) = 1/x$$ at $$x = 2.$$ We can use Equation 3.3, but as we have seen, the results are the same if we use Equation 3.4. $$\begin{array}{clccl} m_{\tan } & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(2)}{x - 2}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 2}} & & & { \text{Substitute} f(x) = \frac{1}{x} \text{and} f(2) = \frac{1}{2}.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{2}}{x - 2} \cdot \frac{2x}{2x}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Multiply numerator and denominator by} 2x \text{to} } \\ \text{simplify fractions.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{\left( {2 - x} \right)}{\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {2x} \right)}} & & & \text{Simplify.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{-1}{2x}} & & & { \text{Simplify using} \frac{2 - x}{x - 2} = -1, \text{for} x \neq 2.} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{4}} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$ We now know that the slope of the tangent line is $$- \frac{1}{4}.$$ To find an equation of the tangent line, we also need a point on the line. We know that $$f(2) = \frac{1}{2}.$$ Since the tangent line passes through the point $$(2,\frac{1}{2})$$ we can use the point-slope equation of a line to find an equation of the tangent line. Thus the tangent line has the equation $$y = - \frac{1}{4}x + 1.$$ The graphs of $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$ and $$y = - \frac{1}{4}x + 1$$ are shown in Figure 3.7.

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Let f(x) be a function defined in an open interval containing a. The derivative of the function f(x) at a, denoted by f^{\prime}(a), is defined by f^{\prime}(a) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}...
body_xml:
<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be a function defined in an open interval containing $$a.$$ The derivative of the function $$f(x)$$ at $$a,$$ denoted by $$f^{\prime}(a),$$ is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(a) = \underset{x\rightarrow a}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>provided this limit exists.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Alternatively, we may also define the derivative of $$f(x)$$ at $$a$$ as</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(a) = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding a Derivative
snippet: Finding a Derivative: For f(x) = 3x^{2} - 4x + 1, find f^{\prime}(2) by using Equation 3.5. Substitute the given function and value directly into the equation. \begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(2)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim...
body_xml:
<example number="3.5" title="Finding a Derivative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For $$f(x) = 3x^{2} - 4x + 1,$$ find $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ by using Equation 3.5.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Substitute the given function and value directly into the equation.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(2)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(2)}{x - 2}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{\left( {3x^{2} - 4x + 1} \right) - 5}{x - 2}} & & & { \text{Substitute} f(x) = 3x^{2} - 4x + 1 \text{and} f(2) = 5.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }\frac{(x - 2)(3x + 2)}{x - 2}} & & & \text{Simplify and factor the numerator.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 2}{\lim }(3x + 2)} & & & \text{Cancel the common factor.} \\ & {= 8} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Revisiting the Derivative
snippet: Revisiting the Derivative: For f(x) = 3x^{2} - 4x + 1, find f^{\prime}(2) by using Equation 3.6. Using this equation, we can substitute two values of the function into the equation, and we should get the same value as in Example 3.5....
body_xml:
<example number="3.6" title="Revisiting the Derivative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For $$f(x) = 3x^{2} - 4x + 1,$$ find $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ by using Equation 3.6.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Using this equation, we can substitute two values of the function into the equation, and we should get the same value as in Example 3.5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(2)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {2 + h} \right) - f(2)}{h}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{(3{(2 + h)}^{2} - 4\left( {2 + h} \right) + 1) - 5}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} f(2) = 5 \text{and} } \\ {f\left( {2 + h} \right) = 3{(2 + h)}^{2} - 4\left( {2 + h} \right) + 1.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{3h^{2} + 8h}{h}} & & & \text{Simplify the numerator.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h(3h + 8)}{h}} & & & \text{Factor the numerator.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }(3h + 8)} & & & \text{Cancel the common factor.} \\ & {= 8} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The results are the same whether we use Equation 3.5 or Equation 3.6.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Estimating Velocity
snippet: Estimating Velocity: A lead weight on a spring is oscillating up and down. Its position at time t with respect to a fixed horizontal line is given by s(t) = \sin t (Figure 3.9). Use a table of values to estimate v(0). Check the estimate by...
body_xml:
A lead weight on a spring is oscillating up and down. Its position at time $$t$$ with respect to a fixed horizontal line is given by $$s(t) = \sin t$$ (Figure 3.9). Use a table of values to estimate $$v(0).$$ Check the estimate by using Equation 3.5. We can estimate the instantaneous velocity at $$t = 0$$ by computing a table of average velocities using values of $$t$$ approaching $$0,$$ as shown in Table 3.1. $$t$$ $$\frac{\sin t - \sin 0}{t - 0} = \frac{\sin t}{t}$$ $$-0.1$$ $$0.998334166$$ $$-0.01$$ $$0.9999833333$$ $$-0.001$$ $$0.999999833$$ $$0.001$$ $$0.999999833$$ $$0.01$$ $$0.9999833333$$ $$0.1$$ $$0.998334166$$
From the table we see that the average velocity over the time interval $$\left\lbrack {-0.1,0} \right\rbrack$$ is $$0.998334166,$$ the average velocity over the time interval $$\left\lbrack {-0.01,0} \right\rbrack$$ is $$0.9999833333,$$ and so forth. Using this table of values, it appears that a good estimate is $$v(0) = 1.$$ By using Equation 3.5, we can see that $$v(0) = s^{\prime}(0) = \underset{t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin t - \sin 0}{t - 0} = \underset{t\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sin t}{t} = 1.$$ Thus, in fact, $$v(0) = 1.$$

title: Chapter Opener: Estimating Rate of Change of Velocity
snippet: Chapter Opener: Estimating Rate of Change of Velocity: Reaching a top speed of 270.49 mph, the Hennessey Venom GT is one of the fastest cars in the world. In tests it went from 0 to 60 mph in 3.05 seconds, from 0 \text{to} 100 mph in 5.88...
body_xml:
Reaching a top speed of $$270.49$$ mph, the Hennessey Venom GT is one of the fastest cars in the world. In tests it went from $$0$$ to $$60$$ mph in $$3.05$$ seconds, from $$0 \text{to} 100$$ mph in $$5.88$$ seconds, from $$0 \text{to} 200$$ mph in $$14.51$$ seconds, and from $$0 \text{to} 229.9$$ mph in $$19.96$$ seconds. Use this data to draw a conclusion about the rate of change of velocity (that is, its acceleration) as it approaches $$229.9$$ mph. Does the rate at which the car is accelerating appear to be increasing, decreasing, or constant? First observe that $$60$$ mph = $$88$$ ft/s, $$100$$ mph $$\approx 146.67$$ ft/s, $$200$$ mph $$\approx 293.33$$ ft/s, and $$229.9$$ mph $$\approx 337.19$$ ft/s. We can summarize the information in a table. $$t$$ $$v(t)$$ $$0$$ $$0$$ $$3.05$$ $$88$$ $$5.88$$ $$146.67$$ $$14.51$$ $$293.33$$ $$19.96$$ $$337.19$$
Now compute the average acceleration of the car in feet per second per second on intervals of the form $$\left\lbrack {t,19.96} \right\rbrack$$ as $$t$$ approaches $$19.96,$$ as shown in the following table. $$t$$ $$\frac{v(t) - v(19.96)}{t - 19.96} = \frac{v(t) - 337.19}{t - 19.96}$$ $$0.0$$ $$16.89$$ $$3.05$$ $$14.74$$ $$5.88$$ $$13.53$$ $$14.51$$ $$8.05$$
The rate at which the car is accelerating is decreasing as its velocity approaches $$229.9$$ mph $$(337.19$$ ft/s).

title: Rate of Change of Temperature
snippet: Rate of Change of Temperature: A homeowner sets the thermostat so that the temperature in the house begins to drop from 70^\circ \text{F} at 9 p.m., reaches a low of 60^\circ during the night, and rises back to 70^\circ by 7 a.m. the next...
body_xml:
<example number="3.9" title="Rate of Change of Temperature">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A homeowner sets the thermostat so that the temperature in the house begins to drop from $$70^\circ \text{F}$$ at $$9$$ p.m., reaches a low of $$60^\circ$$ during the night, and rises back to $$70^\circ$$ by $$7$$ a.m. the next morning. Suppose that the temperature in the house is given by $$T(t) = 0.4t^{2} - 4t + 70$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 10,$$ where $$t$$ is the number of hours past $$9$$ p.m. Find the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at midnight.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since midnight is $$3$$ hours past $$9$$ p.m., we want to compute $$T^{\prime}(3).$$ Refer to Equation 3.5.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {T^{\prime}(3)} & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{T(t) - T(3)}{t - 3}} & & & \text{Apply the definition.} \\ & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{0.4t^{2} - 4t + 70 - 61.6}{t - 3}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} T(t) = 0.4t^{2} - 4t + 70 \text{and} } \\ {T(3) = 61.6.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{0.4t^{2} - 4t + 8.4}{t - 3}} & & & \text{Simplify.} \\ & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{0.4(t - 3)(t - 7)}{t - 3}} & & & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }\frac{0.4(t - 3)(t - 7)}{t - 3}} \\ & {= \underset{t\rightarrow 3}{\lim }0.4(t - 7)} & & & \text{Cancel.} \\ & {= -1.6} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at midnight is $$-1.6^\circ \text{F}$$ per hour.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Rate of Change of Profit
snippet: Rate of Change of Profit: A toy company can sell x electronic gaming systems at a price of p = -0.01x + 400 dollars per gaming system. The cost of manufacturing x systems is given by C(x) = 100x + 10,000 dollars. Find the rate of change of...
body_xml:
<example number="3.10" title="Rate of Change of Profit">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A toy company can sell $$x$$ electronic gaming systems at a price of $$p = -0.01x + 400$$ dollars per gaming system. The cost of manufacturing $$x$$ systems is given by $$C(x) = 100x + 10,000$$ dollars. Find the rate of change of profit when $$10,000$$ games are produced. Should the toy company increase or decrease production?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The profit $$P(x)$$ earned by producing $$x$$ gaming systems is $$R(x) - C(x),$$ where $$R(x)$$ is the revenue obtained from the sale of $$x$$ games. Since the company can sell $$x$$ games at $$p = -0.01x + 400$$ per game,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$R(x) = xp = x\left( {-0.01x + 400} \right) = -0.01x^{2} + 400x.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Consequently,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P(x) = -0.01x^{2} + 300x - 10,000.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, evaluating the rate of change of profit gives</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {P^{\prime}(10000)} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 10000}{\lim }\frac{P(x) - P(10000)}{x - 10000}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 10000}{\lim }\frac{-0.01x^{2} + 300x - 10000 - 1990000}{x - 10000}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow 10000}{\lim }\frac{-0.01x^{2} + 300x - 2000000}{x - 10000}} \\ & {= 100.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since the rate of change of profit $$P^{\prime}(10,000) > 0$$ and $$P(10,000) > 0,$$ the company should increase production.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Derivative of a Square-Root Function
snippet: Finding the Derivative of a Square-Root Function: Find the derivative of f(x) = \sqrt{x}. Start directly with the definition of the derivative function. Use Equation 3.1. \begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow...
body_xml:
<example number="3.11" title="Finding the Derivative of a Square-Root Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the derivative of $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start directly with the definition of the derivative function. Use Equation 3.1.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} f\left( {x + h} \right) = \sqrt{x + h} \text{and} f(x) = \sqrt{x}} \\ { \text{into} f^{\prime}(x) = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}} & & & \begin{array}{l} \text{Multiply numerator and denominator by} \\ {\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x} \text{without distributing in the} } \\ \text{denominator.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h}{h(\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x})}} & & & \text{Multiply the numerators and simplify.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{1}{(\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x})}} & & & { \text{Cancel the} h.} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Derivative of a Quadratic Function
snippet: Finding the Derivative of a Quadratic Function: Find the derivative of the function f(x) = x^{2} - 2x. Follow the same procedure here, but without having to multiply by the conjugate. \begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {=...
body_xml:
<example number="3.12" title="Finding the Derivative of a Quadratic Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the derivative of the function $$f(x) = x^{2} - 2x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Follow the same procedure here, but without having to multiply by the conjugate.</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{({(x + h)}^{2} - 2\left( {x + h} \right)) - (x^{2} - 2x)}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} f\left( {x + h} \right) = {(x + h)}^{2} - 2(x + h) \text{and} } \\ {f(x) = x^{2} - 2x \text{into} } \\ {f^{\prime}(x) = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 2x - 2h - x^{2} + 2x}{h}} & & & { \text{Expand} {(x + h)}^{2} - 2(x + h).} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{2xh - 2h + h^{2}}{h}} & & & \text{Simplify.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h(2x - 2 + h)}{h}} & & & { \text{Factor out} h \text{from the numerator.} } \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }(2x - 2 + h)} & & & { \text{Cancel the common factor of} h.} \\ & {= 2x - 2} & & & \text{Evaluate the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: A Piecewise Function that is Continuous and Differentiable
snippet: A Piecewise Function that is Continuous and Differentiable: A toy company wants to design a track for a toy car that starts out along a parabolic curve and then converts to a straight line (Figure 3.17). The function that describes the...
body_xml: A toy company wants to design a track for a toy car that starts out along a parabolic curve and then converts to a straight line (Figure 3.17). The function that describes the track is to have the form $$f(x) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {\frac{1}{10}x^{2} + bx + c \text{if} x < -10} \\ {- \frac{1}{4}x + \frac{5}{2} \text{if} x \geq -10} \end{matrix} \right.$$ where $$x$$ and $$f(x)$$ are in inches. For the car to move smoothly along the track, the function $$f(x)$$ must be both continuous and differentiable at $$-10.$$ Find values of $$b$$ and $$c$$ that make $$f(x)$$ both continuous and differentiable. For the function to be continuous at $$x = -10,\underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = f(-10).$$ Thus, since $$\underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }f(x) = \frac{1}{10}{(-10)}^{2} - 10b + c = 10 - 10b + c$$ and $$f(-10) = 5,$$ we must have $$10 - 10b + c = 5.$$ Equivalently, we have $$c = 10b - 5.$$ For the function to be differentiable at $$-10,$$ $$f^{\prime}(-10) = \underset{x\rightarrow-10}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(-10)}{x + 10}$$ must exist. Since $$f(x)$$ is defined using different rules on the right and the left, we must evaluate this limit from the right and the left and then set them equal to each other: $$\begin{array}{clccc} {\underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(-10)}{x + 10}} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{10}x^{2} + bx + c - 5}{x + 10}} & & & \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }\frac{\frac{1}{10}x^{2} + bx + \left( {10b - 5} \right) - 5}{x + 10}} & & & { \text{Substitute} c = 10b - 5.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }\frac{x^{2} - 100 + 10bx + 100b}{10(x + 10)}} & & & \text{Multiply numerator and denominator by 10.} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{-}}{\lim }\frac{(x + 10)(x - 10 + 10b)}{10(x + 10)}} & & & \text{Factor by grouping.} \\ & {= b - 2.} & & & \end{array}$$ We also have $$\begin{array}{cl} {\underset{x\rightarrow-10^{+}}{\lim }\frac{f(x) - f(-10)}{x + 10}} & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{+}}{\lim }\frac{- \frac{1}{4}x + \frac{5}{2} - 5}{x + 10}} \\ & {= \underset{x\rightarrow-10^{+}}{\lim }\frac{-(x + 10)}{4(x + 10)}} \\ & {= - \frac{1}{4}.} \end{array}$$ This gives us $$b - 2 = - \frac{1}{4}.$$ Thus $$b = \frac{7}{4}$$ and $$c = 10\left( \frac{7}{4} \right) - 5 = \frac{25}{2}.$$

snippet: Finding a Second Derivative: For f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3x + 1, find f^{''}(x). First find f^{\prime}(x). \begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {2{(x + h)}^{2} - 3\left( {x + h} \right) + 1}...
body_xml:
<example number="3.15" title="Finding a Second Derivative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For $$f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3x + 1,$$ find $$f^{''}(x).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First find $$f^{\prime}(x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{\prime}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {2{(x + h)}^{2} - 3\left( {x + h} \right) + 1} \right) - (2x^{2} - 3x + 1)}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} f(x) = 2x^{2} - 3x + 1} \\ \text{and} \\ {f\left( {x + h} \right) = 2{(x + h)}^{2} - 3\left( {x + h} \right) + 1} \\ { \text{into} f^{\prime}(x) = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h}.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{4xh + 2h^{2} - 3h}{h}} & & & \text{Simplify the numerator.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\left( {4x + 2h - 3} \right)} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Factor out the} h \text{in the numerator} } \\ { \text{and cancel with the} h \text{in the} } \\ \text{denominator.} \end{array} \\ & {= 4x - 3} & & & \text{Take the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, find $$f^{''}(x)$$ by taking the derivative of $$f^{\prime}(x) = 4x - 3.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccl} {f^{''}(x)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f^{\prime}\left( {x + h} \right) - f^{\prime}(x)}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Use} f^{\prime}(x) = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)}{h} \text{with} f^{\prime}(x) \text{in} } \\ { \text{place of} f(x).} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{\left( {4\left( {x + h} \right) - 3} \right) - (4x - 3)}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{Substitute} f^{\prime}\left( {x + h} \right) = 4\left( {x + h} \right) - 3 \text{and} } \\ {f^{\prime}(x) = 4x - 3.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }4} & & & \text{Simplify.} \\ & {= 4} & & & \text{Take the limit.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding Acceleration
snippet: Finding Acceleration: The position of a particle along a coordinate axis at time t (in seconds) is given by s(t) = 3t^{2} - 4t + 1 (in meters). Find the function that describes its acceleration at time t. Since v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) and...
body_xml:
<example number="3.16" title="Finding Acceleration">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The position of a particle along a coordinate axis at time $$t$$ (in seconds) is given by $$s(t) = 3t^{2} - 4t + 1$$ (in meters). Find the function that describes its acceleration at time $$t.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Since $$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t)$$ and $$a(t) = v^{\prime}(t) = s^{''}(t),$$ we begin by finding the derivative of $$s(t):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {s^{\prime}(t)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{s\left( {t + h} \right) - s(t)}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{3\left( {t + h} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {t + h} \right) + 1 - \left( {3t^{2} - 4t + 1} \right)}{h}} \\ & {= 6t - 4.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {s^{''}(t)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{s^{\prime}\left( {t + h} \right) - s^{\prime}(t)}{h}} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{6\left( {t + h} \right) - 4 - (6t - 4)}{h}} \\ & {= 6.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, $$a = 6{ \text{m/s} }^{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Differentiating x3x3: Find \frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right). \begin{array}{clccc} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{{(x + h)}^{3} - x^{3}}{h}} & & & \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim...
body_xml:
<example number="3.18" title="Differentiating x3x3">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{clccc} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right)} & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{{(x + h)}^{3} - x^{3}}{h}} & & & \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{x^{3} + 3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3} - x^{3}}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} \text{Notice that the first term in the expansion of} \\ {{(x + h)}^{3} \text{is} x^{3} \text{and the second term is} 3x^{2}h. \text{All} } \\ { \text{other terms contain powers of} h \text{that are two or} } \\ \text{greater.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3}}{h}} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{In this step the} x^{3} \text{terms have been cancelled,} } \\ { \text{leaving only terms containing} h.} \end{array} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }\frac{h(3x^{2} + 3xh + h^{2})}{h}} & & & { \text{Factor out the common factor of} h.} \\ & {= \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim }(3x^{2} + 3xh + h^{2})} & & & \begin{array}{l} { \text{After cancelling the common factor of} h, \text{the} } \\ { \text{only term not containing} h \text{is} 3x^{2}.} \end{array} \\ & {= 3x^{2}} & & & { \text{Let} h \text{go to 0.} } \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules
snippet: Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules: Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules Let f(x) and g(x) be differentiable functions and k be a constant. Then each of the following equations holds. Sum Rule. The derivative of the sum...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="3.4" title="Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules">
    <heading level="4">Sum, Difference, and Constant Multiple Rules</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ and $$g(x)$$ be differentiable functions and $$k$$ be a constant. Then each of the following equations holds.</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Sum Rule. The derivative of the sum of a function $$f$$ and a function $$g$$ is the same as the sum of the derivative of $$f$$ and the derivative of $$g.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {f(x) + g(x)} \right) = \frac{d}{dx}\left( {f(x)} \right) + \frac{d}{dx}\left( {g(x)} \right);$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>that is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{for} j(x) = f(x) + g(x),j^{\prime}(x) = f^{\prime}(x) + g^{\prime}(x).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Difference Rule. The derivative of the difference of a function f and a function g is the same as the difference of the derivative of f and the derivative of $$g:$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {f(x) - g(x)} \right) = \frac{d}{dx}\left( {f(x)} \right) - \frac{d}{dx}\left( {g(x)} \right);$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>that is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\text{for} j(x) = f(x) - g(x),j^{\prime}(x) = f^{\prime}(x) - g^{\prime}(x).$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Constant Multiple Rule. The derivative of a constant k multiplied by a function f is the same as the constant multiplied by the derivative: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {kf(x)} \right) = k\frac{d}{dx}\left( {f(x)} \right);$$</paragraph>

      <paragraph>To find an equation of the tangent line, we need a point and a slope. To find the point, compute</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left( {1,3} \right).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>This gives us the point $$f^{\prime}(1),$$ Since the slope of the tangent line at 1 is $$f^{\prime}(x).$$ we must first find $$f^{\prime}(x) = 2x - 4$$ Using the definition of a derivative, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(1) = -2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so the slope of the tangent line is $$y - 3 = -2\left( {x - 1} \right).$$ Using the point-slope formula, we see that the equation of the tangent line is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = -2x + 5.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Putting the equation of the line in slope-intercept form, we obtain</paragraph>

title: Comparing Instantaneous Velocity and Average Velocity
snippet: Comparing Instantaneous Velocity and Average Velocity: A ball is dropped from a height of 64 feet. Its height above ground (in feet) t seconds later is given by s(t) = -16t^{2} + 64. What is the instantaneous velocity of the ball when it...
body_xml:
<example number="3.34" title="Comparing Instantaneous Velocity and Average Velocity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A ball is dropped from a height of 64 feet. Its height above ground (in feet) $$t$$ seconds later is given by $$s(t) = -16t^{2} + 64.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>What is the instantaneous velocity of the ball when it hits the ground?</item>
        <item>What is the average velocity during its fall?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first thing to do is determine how long it takes the ball to reach the ground. To do this, set $$s(t) = 0.$$ Solving $$-16t^{2} + 64 = 0,$$ we get $$t = 2,$$ so it take 2 seconds for the ball to reach the ground.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The instantaneous velocity of the ball as it strikes the ground is $$v(2).$$ Since $$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = -32t,$$ we obtain $$v(t) = -64 \text{ft/s} .$$</item>
        <item>The average velocity of the ball during its fall is $$v_{ave} = \frac{s(2) - s(0)}{2 - 0} = \frac{0 - 64}{2} = -32 \text{ft/s} .$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Interpreting the Relationship between v(t)v(t) and a(t)a(t)
snippet: Interpreting the Relationship between v(t)v(t) and a(t)a(t): A particle moves along a coordinate axis in the positive direction to the right. Its position at time t is given by s(t) = t^{3} - 4t + 2. Find v(1) and a(1) and use these values...
body_xml:
<example number="3.35" title="Interpreting the Relationship between v(t)v(t) and a(t)a(t)">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A particle moves along a coordinate axis in the positive direction to the right. Its position at time $$t$$ is given by $$s(t) = t^{3} - 4t + 2.$$ Find $$v(1)$$ and $$a(1)$$ and use these values to answer the following questions.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Is the particle moving from left to right or from right to left at time $$t = 1?$$</item>
        <item>Is the particle speeding up or slowing down at time $$t = 1?$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Begin by finding $$v(t)$$ and $$a(t).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>$$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2} - 4$$ and $$a(t) = v^{\prime}(t) = s^{''}(t) = 6t.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Evaluating these functions at $$t = 1,$$ we obtain $$v(1) = -1$$ and $$a(1) = 6.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Because $$v(1) < 0,$$ the particle is moving from right to left.</item>
        <item>Because $$v(1) < 0$$ and $$a(1) > 0,$$ velocity and acceleration are acting in opposite directions. In other words, the particle is being accelerated in the direction opposite the direction in which it is traveling, causing $$\left| {v(t)} \right|$$ to decrease. The particle is slowing down.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Position and Velocity: The position of a particle moving along a coordinate axis is given by s(t) = t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 24t + 4,t \geq 0. Find v(t). At what time(s) is the particle at rest? On what time intervals is the particle moving from...
body_xml:
<example number="3.36" title="Position and Velocity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The position of a particle moving along a coordinate axis is given by $$s(t) = t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 24t + 4,t \geq 0.$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Find $$v(t).$$</item>
        <item>At what time(s) is the particle at rest?</item>
        <item>On what time intervals is the particle moving from left to right? From right to left?</item>
        <item>Use the information obtained to sketch the path of the particle along a coordinate axis.</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The velocity is the derivative of the position function: $$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = 3t^{2} - 18t + 24.$$</item>
        <item>The particle is at rest when $$v(t) = 0,$$ so set $$3t^{2} - 18t + 24 = 0.$$ Factoring the left-hand side of the equation produces $$3\left( {t - 2} \right)\left( {t - 4} \right) = 0.$$ Solving, we find that the particle is at rest at $$t = 2$$ and $$t = 4.$$</item>
        <item>The particle is moving from left to right when $$v(t) > 0$$ and from right to left when $$v(t) < 0.$$ Figure 3.23 gives the analysis of the sign of $$v(t)$$ for $$t \geq 0,$$ but it does not represent the axis along which the particle is moving. Figure 3.23 The sign of v(t) determines the direction of the particle. Since $$3t^{2} - 18t + 24 > 0$$ on $$\lbrack 0,2) \cup (4,+\infty),$$ the particle is moving from left to right on these intervals. Since $$3t^{2} - 18t + 24 < 0$$ on $$\left( {2,4} \right),$$ the particle is moving from right to left on this interval.</item>
        <item>Before we can sketch the graph of the particle, we need to know its position at the time it starts moving $$\left( t = 0) \right.$$ and at the times that it changes direction $$\left( {t = 2,4} \right).$$ We have $$s(0) = 4,s(2) = 24,$$ and $$s(4) = 20.$$ This means that the particle begins on the coordinate axis at 4 and changes direction at 24 and 20 on the coordinate axis. The path of the particle is shown on a coordinate axis in Figure 3.24. Figure 3.24 The path of the particle can be determined by analyzing v(t).</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Estimating a Population: The population of a city is tripling every 5 years. If its current population is 10,000, what will be its approximate population 2 years from now? Let P(t) be the population (in thousands) t years from now. Thus,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.37" title="Estimating a Population">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>The population of a city is tripling every 5 years. If its current population is 10,000, what will be its approximate population 2 years from now?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$P(t)$$ be the population (in thousands) $$t$$ years from now. Thus, we know that $$P(0) = 10$$ and based on the information, we anticipate $$P(5) = 30.$$ Now estimate $$P^{\prime}(0),$$ the current growth rate, using</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P^{\prime}(0) \approx \frac{P(5) - P(0)}{5 - 0} = \frac{30 - 10}{5} = 4.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>By applying Equation 3.10 to $$P(t),$$ we can estimate the population 2 years from now by writing</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$P(2) \approx P(0) + (2)P^{\prime}(0) \approx 10 + 2(4) = 18;$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>thus, in 2 years the population will be 18,000.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph>If $$P(x) = R(x) - C(x)$$ is the profit obtained from selling x items, then the marginal profit $$MP(x)$$ is defined to be $$MP(x) = P^{\prime}(x) = MR(x) - MC(x) = R^{\prime}(x) - C^{\prime}(x).$$</paragraph>

snippet: Applying Marginal Revenue: Assume that the number of barbeque dinners that can be sold, x, can be related to the price charged, p, by the equation p(x) = 9 - 0.03x,0 \leq x \leq 300. In this case, the revenue in dollars obtained by selling...

<example number="3.38" title="Applying Marginal Revenue">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Assume that the number of barbeque dinners that can be sold, $$x,$$ can be related to the price charged, $$p,$$ by the equation $$p(x) = 9 - 0.03x,0 \leq x \leq 300.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In this case, the revenue in dollars obtained by selling $$x$$ barbeque dinners is given by</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$R(x) = xp(x) = x\left( {9 - 0.03x} \right) = -0.03x^{2} + 9x \text{for} 0 \leq x \leq 300.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Use the marginal revenue function to estimate the revenue obtained from selling the 101st barbeque dinner. Compare this to the actual revenue obtained from the sale of this dinner.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First, find the marginal revenue function: $$MR(x) = R^{\prime}(x) = -0.06x + 9.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, use $$R^{\prime}(100)$$ to approximate $$R(101) - R(100),$$ the revenue obtained from the sale of the 101st dinner. Since $$R^{\prime}(100) = 3,$$ the revenue obtained from the sale of the 101st dinner is approximately \$3.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The actual revenue obtained from the sale of the 101st dinner is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$R(101) - R(100) = 602.97 - 600 = 2.97, \text{or} \$ 2.97.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The marginal revenue is a fairly good estimate in this case and has the advantage of being easy to compute.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="3.41" title="An Application to Velocity">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A particle moves along a coordinate axis in such a way that its position at time $$t$$ is given by $$s(t) = 2\sin t - t$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$ At what times is the particle at rest?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To determine when the particle is at rest, set $$s^{\prime}(t) = v(t) = 0.$$ Begin by finding $$s^{\prime}(t).$$ We obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$s^{\prime}(t) = 2\cos t - 1,$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>so we must solve</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$2\cos t - 1 = 0 \text{for} 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The solutions to this equation are $$t = \frac{\pi}{3}$$ and $$t = \frac{5\pi}{3}.$$ Thus the particle is at rest at times $$t = \frac{\pi}{3}$$ and $$t = \frac{5\pi}{3}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: The Derivative of the Tangent Function
snippet: The Derivative of the Tangent Function: Find the derivative of f(x) = \tan x. Start by expressing \tan x as the quotient of \sin x and \cos x: f(x) = \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}. Now apply the quotient rule to obtain f^{\prime}(x) =...
body_xml:
<example number="3.42" title="The Derivative of the Tangent Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the derivative of $$f(x) = \tan x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Start by expressing $$\tan x$$ as the quotient of $$\sin x$$ and $$\cos x:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now apply the quotient rule to obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\cos x\cos x - (-\sin x)\sin x}{\left( {\cos x} \right)^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Simplifying, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{\cos^{2}x + { \sin }^{2}x}{\cos^{2}x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Recognizing that $$\cos^{2}x + \sin^{2}x = 1,$$ by the Pythagorean theorem, we now have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{1}{\cos^{2}x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Finally, use the identity $$\sec x = \frac{1}{\cos x}$$ to obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \sec^{2}x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line
snippet: Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line: Find the equation of a line tangent to the graph of f(x) = \cot x at x = \frac{ \text{π} }{4}. To find an equation of the tangent line, we need a point and a slope at that point. To find the point,...
body_xml:
<example number="3.43" title="Finding the Equation of a Tangent Line">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the equation of a line tangent to the graph of $$f(x) = \cot x$$ at $$x = \frac{ \text{π} }{4}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find an equation of the tangent line, we need a point and a slope at that point. To find the point, compute</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = \cot \frac{\pi}{4} = 1.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus the tangent line passes through the point $$\left( {\frac{\pi}{4},1} \right).$$ Next, find the slope by finding the derivative of $$f(x) = \cot x$$ and evaluating it at $$\frac{\pi}{4}:$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = -\csc^{2}x \text{and} f^{\prime}\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = -\csc^{2}\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = -2.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the point-slope equation of the line, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y - 1 = -2\left( {x - \frac{\pi}{4}} \right)$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>or equivalently,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$y = -2x + 1 + \frac{\pi}{2}.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding the Derivative of Trigonometric Functions
snippet: Finding the Derivative of Trigonometric Functions: Find the derivative of f(x) = \csc x + x\tan x. To find this derivative, we must use both the sum rule and the product rule. Using the sum rule, we find f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="3.44" title="Finding the Derivative of Trigonometric Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the derivative of $$f(x) = \csc x + x\tan x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find this derivative, we must use both the sum rule and the product rule. Using the sum rule, we find</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left( {\csc x} \right) + \frac{d}{dx}(x\tan x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>In the first term, $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\csc x} \right) = -\csc x\cot x,$$ and by applying the product rule to the second term we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}(x\tan x) = (1)(\tan x) + (\sec^{2}x)(x).$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Therefore, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f^{\prime}(x) = -\csc x\cot x + \tan x + x\sec^{2}x.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding Higher-Order Derivatives of y=sinxy=sinx
snippet: Finding Higher-Order Derivatives of y=sinxy=sinx: Find the first four derivatives of y = \sin x. Each step in the chain is straightforward: \begin{array}{rll} y & = & {\sin x} \\ \frac{dy}{dx} & = & {\cos x} \\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} & = &...
body_xml:
<example number="3.45" title="Finding Higher-Order Derivatives of y=sinxy=sinx">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the first four derivatives of $$y = \sin x.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Each step in the chain is straightforward:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} y & = & {\sin x} \\ \frac{dy}{dx} & = & {\cos x} \\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} & = & {-\sin x} \\ \frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}} & = & {-\cos x} \\ \frac{d^{4}y}{dx^{4}} & = & {\sin x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>Once we recognize the pattern of derivatives, we can find any higher-order derivative by determining the step in the pattern to which it corresponds. For example, every fourth derivative of sin x equals sin x, so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d^{4}}{dx^{4}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \frac{d^{8}}{dx^{8}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \frac{d^{12}}{dx^{12}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \text{…} = \frac{d^{4n}}{dx^{4n}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \sin x} \\ {\frac{d^{5}}{dx^{5}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \frac{d^{9}}{dx^{9}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \frac{d^{13}}{dx^{13}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \text{…} = \frac{d^{4n + 1}}{dx^{4n + 1}}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \cos x.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: An Application to Acceleration
snippet: An Application to Acceleration: A particle moves along a coordinate axis in such a way that its position at time t is given by s(t) = 2 - \sin t. Find v\left( {\pi/4} \right) and a\left( {\pi/4} \right). Compare these values and decide...
body_xml:
<example number="3.47" title="An Application to Acceleration">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A particle moves along a coordinate axis in such a way that its position at time $$t$$ is given by $$s(t) = 2 - \sin t.$$ Find $$v\left( {\pi/4} \right)$$ and $$a\left( {\pi/4} \right).$$ Compare these values and decide whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>First find $$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t):$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = -\cos t.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$v\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, find $$a(t) = v^{\prime}(t).$$ Thus, $$a(t) = v^{\prime}(t) = \sin t$$ and we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$a\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since $$v\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} < 0$$ and $$a\left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} > 0,$$ we see that velocity and acceleration are acting in opposite directions; that is, the object is being accelerated in the direction opposite to the direction in which it is travelling. Consequently, the particle is slowing down.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>
