title: General Form of an Antiderivative
snippet: General Form of an Antiderivative: General Form of an Antiderivative Let F be an antiderivative of f over an interval I. Then, for each constant C, the function F(x) + C is also an antiderivative of f over I; if G is an antiderivative of f...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="4.14" title="General Form of an Antiderivative">
    <heading level="4">General Form of an Antiderivative</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$F$$ be an antiderivative of $$f$$ over an interval $$I.$$ Then,</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>for each constant $$C,$$ the function $$F(x) + C$$ is also an antiderivative of $$f$$ over $$I;$$</item>
      <item>if $$G$$ is an antiderivative of $$f$$ over $$I,$$ there is a constant $$C$$ for which $$G(x) = F(x) + C$$ over $$I.$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>In other words, the most general form of the antiderivative of $$f$$ over $$I$$ is $$F(x) + C.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding Antiderivatives
snippet: Finding Antiderivatives: For each of the following functions, find all antiderivatives. f(x) = 3x^{2} f(x) = \frac{1}{x} f(x) = \cos x f(x) = e^{x} Because \frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right) = 3x^{2} then F(x) = x^{3} is an antiderivative of...
body_xml:
<example number="4.50" title="Finding Antiderivatives">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>For each of the following functions, find all antiderivatives.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$f(x) = 3x^{2}$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = \cos x$$</item>
        <item>$$f(x) = e^{x}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Because $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( x^{3} \right) = 3x^{2}$$ then $$F(x) = x^{3}$$ is an antiderivative of $$3x^{2}.$$ Therefore, every antiderivative of $$3x^{2}$$ is of the form $$x^{3} + C$$ for some constant $$C,$$ and every function of the form $$x^{3} + C$$ is an antiderivative of $$3x^{2}.$$</item>
        <item>Let $$f(x) = \ln |x|.$$ For $$x > 0,f(x) = \ln (x)$$ and $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\ln x} \right) = \frac{1}{x}.$$ For $$x < 0,f(x) = \ln \left( {-x} \right)$$ and $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\ln \left( {-x} \right)} \right) = - \frac{1}{-x} = \frac{1}{x}.$$ Therefore, $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\ln |x|} \right) = \frac{1}{x}.$$ Thus, $$F(x) = \ln |x|$$ is an antiderivative of $$\frac{1}{x}.$$ Therefore, every antiderivative of $$\frac{1}{x}$$ is of the form $$\ln |x| + C$$ for some constant $$C$$ and every function of the form $$\ln |x| + C$$ is an antiderivative of $$\frac{1}{x}.$$</item>
        <item>We have $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\sin x} \right) = \cos x,$$ so $$F(x) = \sin x$$ is an antiderivative of $$\cos x.$$ Therefore, every antiderivative of $$\cos x$$ is of the form $$\sin x + C$$ for some constant $$C$$ and every function of the form $$\sin x + C$$ is an antiderivative of $$\cos x.$$</item>
        <item>Since $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( e^{x} \right) = e^{x},$$ then $$F(x) = e^{x}$$ is an antiderivative of $$e^{x}.$$ Therefore, every antiderivative of $$e^{x}$$ is of the form $$e^{x} + C$$ for some constant $$C$$ and every function of the form $$e^{x} + C$$ is an antiderivative of $$e^{x}.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Verifying an Indefinite Integral
snippet: Verifying an Indefinite Integral: Each of the following statements is of the form {\int{f(x)dx = F(x) + C}}. Verify that each statement is correct by showing that F^{\prime}(x) = f(x). {\int\left( {x + e^{x}} \right)}dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} +...
body_xml:
<example number="4.51" title="Verifying an Indefinite Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Each of the following statements is of the form $${\int{f(x)dx = F(x) + C}}.$$ Verify that each statement is correct by showing that $$F^{\prime}(x) = f(x).$$</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$${\int\left( {x + e^{x}} \right)}dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + e^{x} + C$$</item>
        <item>$${\int{xe^{x}dx}} = xe^{x} - e^{x} + C$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Since $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {\frac{x^{2}}{2} + e^{x} + C} \right) = x + e^{x},$$ the statement $${\int\left( {x + e^{x}} \right)}dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + e^{x} + C$$ is correct. Note that we are verifying an indefinite integral for a sum. Furthermore, $$\frac{x^{2}}{2}$$ and $$e^{x}$$ are antiderivatives of $$x$$ and $$e^{x},$$ respectively, and the sum of the antiderivatives is an antiderivative of the sum. We discuss this fact again later in this section.</item>
        <item>Using the product rule, we see that $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( {xe^{x} - e^{x} + C} \right) = e^{x} + xe^{x} - e^{x} = xe^{x}.$$ Therefore, the statement $${\int{xe^{x}dx}} = xe^{x} - e^{x} + C$$ is correct. Note that we are verifying an indefinite integral for a product. The antiderivative $$xe^{x} - e^{x}$$ is not a product of the antiderivatives. Furthermore, the product of antiderivatives, $$x^{2}e^{x}/2$$ is not an antiderivative of $$xe^{x}$$ since $$\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{x^{2}e^{x}}{2} \right) = xe^{x} + \frac{x^{2}e^{x}}{2} \neq xe^{x}.$$ In general, the product of antiderivatives is not an antiderivative of a product.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>

snippet: Evaluating Indefinite Integrals: Evaluate each of the following indefinite integrals: \int{\left( {5x^{3} - 7x^{2} + 3x + 4} \right)dx} {\int\frac{x^{2} + 4\sqrt[3]{x}}{x}}dx {\int\frac{4}{1 + x^{2}}}dx \int{\tan x\cos x dx} Using...

<example number="4.52" title="Evaluating Indefinite Integrals">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate each of the following indefinite integrals:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>$$\int{\left( {5x^{3} - 7x^{2} + 3x + 4} \right)dx}$$</item>
        <item>$${\int\frac{x^{2} + 4\sqrt[3]{x}}{x}}dx$$</item>
        <item>$${\int\frac{4}{1 + x^{2}}}dx$$</item>
        <item>$$\int{\tan x\cos x dx}$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Using Properties of Indefinite Integrals, we can integrate each of the four terms in the integrand separately. We obtain $${\int{\left( {5x^{3} - 7x^{2} + 3x + 4} \right)dx}} = {\int{5x^{3}dx -}}{\int{7x^{2}dx}} + {\int{3x dx}} + {\int{4dx}}.$$ From the second part of Properties of Indefinite Integrals, each coefficient can be written in front of the integral sign, which gives $${\int{5x^{3}dx -}}{\int{7x^{2}dx}} + {\int{3x dx}} + {\int{4dx}} = 5{\int{x^{3}dx - 7}}{\int{x^{2}dx}} + 3{\int{x dx}} + 4{\int{1dx.}}$$ Using the power rule for integrals, we conclude that $${\int{\left( {5x^{3} - 7x^{2} + 3x + 4} \right)dx}} = \frac{5}{4}x^{4} - \frac{7}{3}x^{3} + \frac{3}{2}x^{2} + 4x + C.$$</item>
        <item>Rewrite the integrand as $$\frac{x^{2} + 4\sqrt[3]{x}}{x} = \frac{x^{2}}{x} + \frac{4\sqrt[3]{x}}{x}.$$ Then, to evaluate the integral, integrate each of these terms separately. Using the power rule, we have $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int\left( {x + \frac{4}{x^{2/3}}} \right)}dx} & {= {\int{x dx + 4}}{\int x^{-2/3}}dx} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + 4\frac{1}{\left( \frac{-2}{3} \right) + 1}x^{{({-2/3})} + 1} + C} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + 12x^{1/3} + C.} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Using Properties of Indefinite Integrals, write the integral as $$4{\int{\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}dx}}.$$ Then, use the fact that $$\tan^{-1}(x)$$ is an antiderivative of $$\frac{1}{\left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)}$$ to conclude that $${\int{\frac{4}{1 + x^{2}}dx}} = 4\tan^{-1}(x) + C.$$</item>
        <item>Rewrite the integrand as $$\tan x\cos x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\cos x = \sin x.$$ Therefore, $${\int{\tan x\cos x}} = {\int{\sin x}} = -\cos x + C.$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Decelerating Car
snippet: Decelerating Car: A car is traveling at the rate of 88 ft/sec (60 mph) when the brakes are applied. The car begins decelerating at a constant rate of 15 ft/sec2. How many seconds elapse before the car stops? How far does the car travel...
body_xml:
<example number="4.54" title="Decelerating Car">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>A car is traveling at the rate of $$88$$ ft/sec $$(60$$ mph) when the brakes are applied. The car begins decelerating at a constant rate of $$15$$ ft/sec2.</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>How many seconds elapse before the car stops?</item>
        <item>How far does the car travel during that time?</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>First we introduce variables for this problem. Let $$t$$ be the time (in seconds) after the brakes are first applied. Let $$a(t)$$ be the acceleration of the car (in feet per seconds squared) at time $$t.$$ Let $$v(t)$$ be the velocity of the car (in feet per second) at time $$t.$$ Let $$s(t)$$ be the car’s position (in feet) beyond the point where the brakes are applied at time $$t.$$ The car is traveling at a rate of $$88 \text{ft/sec} .$$ Therefore, the initial velocity is $$v(0) = 88$$ ft/sec. Since the car is decelerating, the acceleration is $$a(t) = -15{ \text{ft/s} }^{2}.$$ The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity, $$v^{\prime}(t) = -15.$$ Therefore, we have an initial-value problem to solve: $$v^{\prime}(t) = -15,v(0) = 88.$$ Integrating, we find that $$v(t) = -15t + C.$$ Since $$v(0) = 88,C = 88.$$ Thus, the velocity function is $$v(t) = -15t + 88.$$ To find how long it takes for the car to stop, we need to find the time $$t$$ such that the velocity is zero. Solving $$-15t + 88 = 0,$$ we obtain $$t = \frac{88}{15}$$ sec.</item>
        <item>To find how far the car travels during this time, we need to find the position of the car after $$\frac{88}{15}$$ sec. We know the velocity $$v(t)$$ is the derivative of the position $$s(t).$$ Consider the initial position to be $$s(0) = 0.$$ Therefore, we need to solve the initial-value problem $$s^{\prime}(t) = -15t + 88,s(0) = 0.$$ Integrating, we have $$s(t) = - \frac{15}{2}t^{2} + 88t + C.$$ Since $$s(0) = 0,$$ the constant is $$C = 0.$$ Therefore, the position function is $$s(t) = - \frac{15}{2}t^{2} + 88t.$$ After $$t = \frac{88}{15}$$ sec, the position is $$s\left( \frac{88}{15} \right) \approx 258.133$$ ft.</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Rule: Properties of Sigma Notation
snippet: Rule: Properties of Sigma Notation: Let a_{1},a_{2} \text{,…,} a_{n} and b_{1},b_{2} \text{,…,} b_{n} represent two sequences of terms and let c be a constant. The following properties hold for all positive integers n and for integers m,...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Properties of Sigma Notation" title="Rule: Properties of Sigma Notation">
    <paragraph>Let $$a_{1},a_{2} \text{,…,} a_{n}$$ and $$b_{1},b_{2} \text{,…,} b_{n}$$ represent two sequences of terms and let c be a constant. The following properties hold for all positive integers n and for integers m, with $$1 \leq m \leq n.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}c} = nc$$ (5.1)</item>
      <item>$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{ca_{i}}} = c{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}}$$ (5.2)</item>
      <item>$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {a_{i} + b_{i}} \right)} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}} + {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}b_{i}}$$ (5.3)</item>
      <item>$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\left( {a_{i} - b_{i}} \right)} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}b_{i}}$$ (5.4)</item>
      <item>$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}a_{i}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}a_{i}} + {\sum\limits_{i = m + 1}^{n}a_{i}}$$ (5.5)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Sums and Powers of Integers" title="Rule: Sums and Powers of Integers">
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The sum of n integers is given by $${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i} = 1 + 2 + \text{⋯} + n = \frac{n\left( {n + 1} \right)}{2}.$$</item>
      <item>The sum of consecutive integers squared is given by $${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i^{2}} = 1^{2} + 2^{2} + \text{⋯} + n^{2} = \frac{n\left( {n + 1} \right)\left( {2n + 1} \right)}{6}.$$</item>
      <item>The sum of consecutive integers cubed is given by $${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i^{3}} = 1^{3} + 2^{3} + \text{⋯} + n^{3} = \frac{n^{2}\left( {n + 1} \right)^{2}}{4}.$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="5.2" title="Evaluation Using Sigma Notation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Write using sigma notation and evaluate:</paragraph>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>The sum of the terms $$\left( {i - 3} \right)^{2}$$ for $$i = 1,2 \text{,…,} 200.$$</item>
        <item>The sum of the terms $$\left( {i^{3} - i^{2}} \right)$$ for $$i = 1,2,3,4,5,6.$$</item>
      </list>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <list type="ordered">
        <item>Multiplying out $$\left( {i - 3} \right)^{2},$$ we can break the expression into three terms. $$\begin{array}{cl} {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}\left( {i - 3} \right)^{2}} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}\left( {i^{2} - 6i + 9} \right)}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}i^{2}} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}{6i}} + {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}9}} \\ & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}i^{2}} - 6{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}i} + {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{200}9}} \\ & {= \frac{200\left( {200 + 1} \right)\left( {400 + 1} \right)}{6} - 6\left\lbrack \frac{200\left( {200 + 1} \right)}{2} \right\rbrack + 9(200)} \\ & {= 2,686,700 - 120,600 + 1800} \\ & {= 2,567,900} \end{array}$$</item>
        <item>Use sigma notation property iv. and the rules for the sum of squared terms and the sum of cubed terms. $$\begin{array}{cl} {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{6}\left( {i^{3} - i^{2}} \right)} & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{6}i^{3}} - {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{6}i^{2}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \frac{6^{2}\left( {6 + 1} \right)^{2}}{4} - \frac{6\left( {6 + 1} \right)\left( {2(6) + 1} \right)}{6}} \\ & {= \frac{1764}{4} - \frac{546}{6}} \\ & {= 350} \end{array}$$</item>
      </list>
    </solution>
  </example>

    <paragraph>A set of points $$P = \left\{ x_{i} \right\}$$ for $$i = 0,1,2 \text{,…,} n$$ with $$a = x_{0} < x_{1} < x_{2} < \text{⋯} < x_{n} = b,$$ which divides the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into subintervals of the form $$\left\lbrack {x_{0},x_{1}} \right\rbrack,\left\lbrack {x_{1},x_{2}} \right\rbrack \text{,…,} \left\lbrack {x_{n - 1},x_{n}} \right\rbrack$$ is called a partition of $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$ If the subintervals all have the same width, the set of points forms a regular partition of the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph>On each subinterval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack$$ (for $$\left. i = 1,2,3 \text{,…,} n \right),$$ construct a rectangle with width Δx and height equal to $$f\left( x_{i - 1} \right),$$ which is the function value at the left endpoint of the subinterval. Then the area of this rectangle is $$f\left( x_{i - 1} \right) \text{Δ} x.$$ Adding the areas of all these rectangles, we get an approximate value for A (Figure 5.3). We use the notation Ln to denote that this is a left-endpoint approximation of A using n subintervals.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {A \approx L_{n}} & {= f\left( x_{0} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{1} \right) \text{Δ} x + \text{⋯} + f\left( x_{n - 1} \right) \text{Δ} x} \\ & \\ & \\ & \\ & {= {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( x_{i - 1} \right) \text{Δ} x}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

snippet: Approximating the Area Under a Curve: Use both left-endpoint and right-endpoint approximations to approximate the area under the curve of f(x) = x^{2} on the interval \left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack; use n = 4. First, divide the interval...
body_xml: Use both left-endpoint and right-endpoint approximations to approximate the area under the curve of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack;$$ use $$n = 4.$$ First, divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ into n equal subintervals. Using $$n = 4, \text{Δ} x = \frac{\left( {2 - 0} \right)}{4} = 0.5.$$ This is the width of each rectangle. The intervals $$\left\lbrack {0,0.5} \right\rbrack,\left\lbrack {0.5,1} \right\rbrack,\left\lbrack {1,1.5} \right\rbrack,\left\lbrack {1.5,2} \right\rbrack$$ are shown in Figure 5.6. Using a left-endpoint approximation, the heights are $$f(0) = 0,f(0.5) = 0.25,f(1) = 1,f(1.5) = 2.25.$$ Then, $$\begin{array}{cl} L_{4} & {= f\left( x_{0} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{1} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{2} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{3} \right) \text{Δ} x} \\ & {= 0(0.5) + 0.25(0.5) + 1(0.5) + 2.25(0.5)} \\ & {= 1.75.} \end{array}$$ The right-endpoint approximation is shown in Figure 5.7. The intervals are the same, $$\text{Δ} x = 0.5,$$ but now use the right endpoint to calculate the height of the rectangles. We have $$\begin{array}{cl} R_{4} & {= f\left( x_{1} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{2} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{3} \right) \text{Δ} x + f\left( x_{4} \right) \text{Δ} x} \\ & {= 0.25(0.5) + 1(0.5) + 2.25(0.5) + 4(0.5)} \\ & {= 3.75.} \end{array}$$ The left-endpoint approximation is 1.75; the right-endpoint approximation is 3.75.

A left-endpoint approximation is the Riemann sum $${\sum\limits_{i = 0}^{5}{\sin x_{i}\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right)}}.$$ We have $$\begin{array}{cl} A & {\approx \sin (0)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{6} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{4} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{3} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right) + \sin \left( \frac{5\pi}{12} \right)\left( \frac{\pi}{12} \right)} \\ & {= 0.863.} \end{array}$$

title: Evaluating an Integral Using the Definition
snippet: Evaluating an Integral Using the Definition: Use the definition of the definite integral to evaluate {\int_{0}^{2}{x^{2}dx}}. Use a right-endpoint approximation to generate the Riemann sum. We first want to set up a Riemann sum. Based on...
body_xml:
<example number="5.7" title="Evaluating an Integral Using the Definition">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the definition of the definite integral to evaluate $${\int_{0}^{2}{x^{2}dx}}.$$ Use a right-endpoint approximation to generate the Riemann sum.</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We first want to set up a Riemann sum. Based on the limits of integration, we have $$a = 0$$ and $$b = 2.$$ For $$i = 0,1,2 \text{,…,} n,$$ let $$P = \left\{ x_{i} \right\}$$ be a regular partition of $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack.$$ Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\text{Δ} x = \frac{b - a}{n} = \frac{2}{n}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Since we are using a right-endpoint approximation to generate Riemann sums, for each i, we need to calculate the function value at the right endpoint of the interval $$\left\lbrack {x_{i - 1},x_{i}} \right\rbrack.$$ The right endpoint of the interval is $$x_{i},$$ and since P is a regular partition,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$x_{i} = x_{0} + i \text{Δ} x = 0 + i\left\lbrack \frac{2}{n} \right\rbrack = \frac{2i}{n}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, the function value at the right endpoint of the interval is</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( x_{i} \right) = x_{i}^{2} = \left( \frac{2i}{n} \right)^{2} = \frac{4i^{2}}{n^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then the Riemann sum takes the form</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( x_{i} \right) \text{Δ} x}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{\left( \frac{4i^{2}}{n^{2}} \right)\frac{2}{n}}} = {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\frac{8i^{2}}{n^{3}}} = \frac{8}{n^{3}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the summation formula for $${\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i^{2}},$$ we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( x_{i} \right) \text{Δ} x}} & {= \frac{8}{n^{3}}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}i^{2}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \frac{8}{n^{3}}\left\lbrack \frac{n\left( {n + 1} \right)\left( {2n + 1} \right)}{6} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{8}{n^{3}}\left\lbrack \frac{2n^{3} + 3n^{2} + n}{6} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{16n^{3} + 24n^{2} + 8n}{6n^{3}}} \\ & {= \frac{8}{3} + \frac{4}{n} + \frac{8}{6n^{2}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, to calculate the definite integral, we need to take the limit as $$n\rightarrow\infty.$$ We get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{2}{x^{2}dx}} & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{f\left( x_{i} \right) \text{Δ} x}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\left( {\frac{8}{3} + \frac{4}{n} + \frac{8}{6n^{2}}} \right)} \\ & {= \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\left( \frac{8}{3} \right) + \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\left( \frac{4}{n} \right) + \underset{n\rightarrow\infty}{\lim }\left( \frac{8}{6n^{2}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{8}{3} + 0 + 0 = \frac{8}{3}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Geometric Formulas to Calculate Definite Integrals
snippet: Using Geometric Formulas to Calculate Definite Integrals: Use the formula for the area of a circle to evaluate {\int_{3}^{6}{\sqrt{9 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}}dx}}. The function describes a semicircle with radius 3. To find...
body_xml: Use the formula for the area of a circle to evaluate $${\int_{3}^{6}{\sqrt{9 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}}dx}}.$$ The function describes a semicircle with radius 3. To find $${\int_{3}^{6}{\sqrt{9 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}}dx}},$$ we want to find the area under the curve over the interval $$\left\lbrack {3,6} \right\rbrack.$$ The formula for the area of a circle is $$A = \pi r^{2}.$$ The area of a semicircle is just one-half the area of a circle, or $$A = \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\pi r^{2}.$$ The shaded area in Figure 5.16 covers one-half of the semicircle, or $$A = \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)\pi r^{2}.$$ Thus, $$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\int_{3}^{6}\sqrt{9 - \left( {x - 3} \right)^{2}}} & {= \frac{1}{4}\pi(3)^{2}} \\ & {= \frac{9}{4}\pi} \\ & {\approx 7.069.} \end{array}$$

title: Finding the Net Signed Area
snippet: Finding the Net Signed Area: Find the net signed area between the curve of the function f(x) = 2x and the x-axis over the interval \left\lbrack {-3,3} \right\rbrack. The function produces a straight line that forms two triangles: one from...
body_xml: Find the net signed area between the curve of the function $$f(x) = 2x$$ and the x-axis over the interval $$\left\lbrack {-3,3} \right\rbrack.$$ The function produces a straight line that forms two triangles: one from $$x = -3$$ to $$x = 0$$ and the other from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 3$$ (Figure 5.19). Using the geometric formula for the area of a triangle, $$A = \frac{1}{2}bh,$$ the area of triangle A1, above the axis, is $$A_{1} = \frac{1}{2}3(6) = 9,$$ where 3 is the base and $$2(3) = 6$$ is the height. The area of triangle A2, below the axis, is $$A_{2} = \frac{1}{2}(3)(6) = 9,$$ where 3 is the base and 6 is the height. Thus, the net area is $${\int_{-3}^{3}{2xdx}} = A_{1} - A_{2} = 9 - 9 = 0.$$ If A1 is the area above the x-axis and A2 is the area below the x-axis, then the net area is $$A_{1} - A_{2}.$$ Since the areas of the two triangles are equal, the net area is zero.

title: Definition
snippet: Definition: Let f(x) be an integrable function defined on an interval \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack. Let A1 represent the area between f(x) and the x-axis that lies above the axis and let A2 represent the area between f(x) and the...

<note type="definition" source_type="Definition" title="Definition">
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x)$$ be an integrable function defined on an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack.$$ Let A1 represent the area between $$f(x)$$ and the x-axis that lies above the axis and let A2 represent the area between $$f(x)$$ and the x-axis that lies below the axis. Then, the net signed area between $$f(x)$$ and the x-axis is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} = A_{1} - A_{2}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The total area between $$f(x)$$ and the x-axis is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{a}^{b}\left| {f(x)} \right|dx = A_{1} + A_{2}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding the Total Area
snippet: Finding the Total Area: Find the total area between f(x) = x - 2 and the x-axis over the interval \left\lbrack {0,6} \right\rbrack. Calculate the x-intercept as \left( {2,0} \right) (set y = 0, solve for x). To find the total area, take...
body_xml: Find the total area between $$f(x) = x - 2$$ and the x-axis over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,6} \right\rbrack.$$ Calculate the x-intercept as $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ (set $$y = 0,$$ solve for x). To find the total area, take the area below the x-axis over the subinterval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack$$ and add it to the area above the x-axis on the subinterval $$\left\lbrack {2,6} \right\rbrack$$ (Figure 5.22). We have $${\int_{0}^{6}{\left| \left( {x - 2} \right) \right|dx}} = A_{2} + A_{1}.$$ Then, using the formula for the area of a triangle, we obtain $$A_{2} = \frac{1}{2}bh = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 2$$ $$A_{1} = \frac{1}{2}bh = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 8.$$ The total area, then, is $$A_{1} + A_{2} = 8 + 2 = 10.$$

snippet: Rule: Properties of the Definite Integral: \int_{a}^{a}{f(x)dx = 0} (5.9) If the limits of integration are the same, the integral is just a line and contains no area. {\int_{b}^{a}{f(x)dx}} = -{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} (5.10) If the limits...
body_xml:
<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Properties of the Definite Integral" title="Rule: Properties of the Definite Integral">
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\int_{a}^{a}{f(x)dx = 0}$$ (5.9) If the limits of integration are the same, the integral is just a line and contains no area.</item>
      <item>$${\int_{b}^{a}{f(x)dx}} = -{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$ (5.10) If the limits are reversed, then place a negative sign in front of the integral.</item>
      <item>$${\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {f(x) + g(x)} \right\rbrack dx}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} + {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}}$$ (5.11) The integral of a sum is the sum of the integrals.</item>
      <item>$$\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {f(x) - g(x)} \right\rbrack dx = {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx - {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}}}}}$$ (5.12) The integral of a difference is the difference of the integrals.</item>
      <item>$${\int_{a}^{b}{cf(x)dx}} = c{\int_{a}^{b}{f{(x)dx}}}$$ (5.13) for constant c. The integral of the product of a constant and a function is equal to the constant multiplied by the integral of the function.</item>
      <item>$${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} = {\int_{a}^{c}{f(x)dx}} + {\int_{c}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$ (5.14) Although this formula normally applies when c is between a and b, the formula holds for all values of a, b, and c, provided $$f(x)$$ is integrable on the largest interval.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Comparison Theorem
snippet: Comparison Theorem: Comparison Theorem If f(x) \geq 0 for a \leq x \leq b, then {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} \geq 0. If f(x) \geq g(x) for a \leq x \leq b, then {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} \geq {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}}. If m and M are constants such...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.2" title="Comparison Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Comparison Theorem</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>If $$f(x) \geq 0$$ for $$a \leq x \leq b,$$ then $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} \geq 0.$$</item>
      <item>If $$f(x) \geq g(x)$$ for $$a \leq x \leq b,$$ then $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} \geq {\int_{a}^{b}{g(x)dx}}.$$</item>
      <item>If m and M are constants such that $$m \leq f(x) \leq M$$ for $$a \leq x \leq b,$$ then $$\begin{array}{cl} {m\left( {b - a} \right)} & {\leq {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} \\ & {\leq M\left( {b - a} \right).} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Comparing Two Functions over a Given Interval
snippet: Comparing Two Functions over a Given Interval: Compare f(x) = \sqrt{1 + x^{2}} and g(x) = \sqrt{1 + x} over the interval \left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack. Graphing these functions is necessary to understand how they compare over the...
body_xml: Compare $$f(x) = \sqrt{1 + x^{2}}$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{1 + x}$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ Graphing these functions is necessary to understand how they compare over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$ Initially, when graphed on a graphing calculator, $$f(x)$$ appears to be above $$g(x)$$ everywhere. However, on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack,$$ the graphs appear to be on top of each other. We need to zoom in to see that, on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack,g(x)$$ is above $$f(x).$$ The two functions intersect at $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ (Figure 5.23). We can see from the graph that over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack,g(x) \geq f(x).$$ Comparing the integrals over the specified interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack,$$ we also see that $${\int_{0}^{1}{g(x)dx}} \geq {\int_{0}^{1}{f(x)dx}}$$ (Figure 5.24). The thin, red-shaded area shows just how much difference there is between these two integrals over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack.$$

title: Finding the Average Value of a Linear Function
snippet: Finding the Average Value of a Linear Function: Find the average value of f(x) = x + 1 over the interval \left\lbrack {0,5} \right\rbrack. First, graph the function on the stated interval, as shown in Figure 5.25. The region is a trapezoid...
body_xml: Find the average value of $$f(x) = x + 1$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,5} \right\rbrack.$$ First, graph the function on the stated interval, as shown in Figure 5.25. The region is a trapezoid lying on its side, so we can use the area formula for a trapezoid $$A = \frac{1}{2}h\left( {a + b} \right),$$ where h represents height, and a and b represent the two parallel sides. Then, $$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{0}^{5}x} + 1dx} & {= \frac{1}{2}h\left( {a + b} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{1}{2} \cdot 5 \cdot \left( {1 + 6} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{35}{2}.} \end{array}$$ Thus the average value of the function is $$\frac{1}{5 - 0}{\int_{0}^{5}x} + 1dx = \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{35}{2} = \frac{7}{2}.$$

title: The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals
snippet: The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals: The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals If f(x) is continuous over an interval \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack, then there is at least one point c \in \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack such that f(c) =...

    <heading level="4">The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals</heading>

title: Finding the Average Value of a Function
snippet: Finding the Average Value of a Function: Find the average value of the function f(x) = 8 - 2x over the interval \left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack and find c such that f(c) equals the average value of the function over \lbrack 0,4\rbrack....
body_xml: Find the average value of the function $$f(x) = 8 - 2x$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ and find c such that $$f(c)$$ equals the average value of the function over $$\lbrack 0,4\rbrack.$$ The formula states the mean value of $$f(x)$$ is given by $$\frac{1}{4 - 0}{\int_{0}^{4}{\left( {8 - 2x} \right)dx}}.$$ We can see in Figure 5.26 that the function represents a straight line and forms a right triangle bounded by the x- and y-axes. The area of the triangle is $$A = \frac{1}{2}\left( \text{base} \right)\left( \text{height} \right).$$ We have $$A = \frac{1}{2}(4)(8) = 16.$$ The average value is found by multiplying the area by $$1/\left( {4 - 0} \right).$$ Thus, the average value of the function is $$\frac{1}{4}(16) = 4.$$ Set the average value equal to $$f(c)$$ and solve for c. $$\begin{array}{cll} {8 - 2c} & = & 4 \\ c & = & 2 \end{array}$$ At $$c = 2,f(2) = 4.$$

Thus, $$c = \sqrt{3}$$ (Figure 5.27).

title: Using the Fundamental Theorem and the Chain Rule to Calculate Derivatives
snippet: Using the Fundamental Theorem and the Chain Rule to Calculate Derivatives: Let F(x) = {\int_{1}^{\sqrt{x}}{\sin tdt}}. Find F^{\prime}\left. (x \right). Letting u(x) = \sqrt{x}, we have F(x) = {\int_{1}^{u{(x)}}{\sin tdt}}. Thus, by the...

<example number="5.18" title="Using the Fundamental Theorem and the Chain Rule to Calculate Derivatives">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$F(x) = {\int_{1}^{\sqrt{x}}{\sin tdt}}.$$ Find $$F^{\prime}\left. (x \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Letting $$u(x) = \sqrt{x},$$ we have $$F(x) = {\int_{1}^{u{(x)}}{\sin tdt}}.$$ Thus, by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and the chain rule,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ {F^{\prime}\left. (x \right)} & {= \sin \left( {u(x)} \right)\frac{du}{dx}} \\ & {= \sin \left( {u(x)} \right) \cdot \left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{-1/2}} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{\sin \sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{x}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>

title: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with Two Variable Limits of Integration
snippet: Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with Two Variable Limits of Integration: Let F(x) = {\int_{x}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}. Find F^{\prime}\left. (x \right). We have F(x) = {\int_{x}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}. Both limits of integration are variable, so...
body_xml:
<example number="5.19" title="Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with Two Variable Limits of Integration">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Let $$F(x) = {\int_{x}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}.$$ Find $$F^{\prime}\left. (x \right).$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have $$F(x) = {\int_{x}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}.$$ Both limits of integration are variable, so we need to split this into two integrals. We get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ {F(x)} & {= {\int_{x}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}} \\ & {= {\int_{x}^{0}{t^{3}dt}} + {\int_{0}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}} \\ & {= -{\int_{0}^{x}{t^{3}dt}} + {\int_{0}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Differentiating the first term, we obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack {-{\int_{0}^{x}{t^{3}dt}}} \right\rbrack = -x^{3}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Differentiating the second term, we first let $$u(x) = 2x.$$ Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ {\frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack {\int_{0}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}} \right\rbrack} & {= \frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack {\int_{0}^{u{(x)}}{t^{3}dt}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {u(x)} \right)^{3}\frac{du}{dx}} \\ & {= \left( {2x} \right)^{3} \cdot 2} \\ & {= 16x^{3}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {F^{\prime}\left. (x \right)} & {= \frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack {-{\int_{0}^{x}{t^{3}dt}}} \right\rbrack + \frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack {\int_{0}^{2x}{t^{3}dt}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -x^{3} + 16x^{3}} \\ & {= 15x^{3}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Evaluating an Integral with the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
snippet: Evaluating an Integral with the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: Use The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 to evaluate {\int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {t^{2} - 4} \right)dt}}. Recall the power rule for Antiderivatives: \text{If} y =...
body_xml: Use The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 to evaluate $${\int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {t^{2} - 4} \right)dt}}.$$ Recall the power rule for Antiderivatives: $$\text{If} y = x^{n},\left. \int{x^{n}dx} \right. = \frac{x^{n + 1}}{n + 1} + C.$$ Use this rule to find the antiderivative of the function and then apply the theorem. We have $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {t^{2} - 4} \right)dt}} & {= \frac{t^{3}}{3} - \left. {4t} \right|_{-2}^{2}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{(2)^{3}}{3} - 4(2)} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3} - 4(-2)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{8}{3} - 8} \right) - \left( {- \frac{8}{3} + 8} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{8}{3} - 8 + \frac{8}{3} - 8} \\ & {= \frac{16}{3} - 16} \\ & {= - \frac{32}{3}.} \end{array}$$ Notice that we did not include the “+ C” term when we wrote the antiderivative. The reason is that, according to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2, any antiderivative works. So, for convenience, we chose the antiderivative with $$C = 0.$$ If we had chosen another antiderivative, the constant term would have canceled out. This always happens when evaluating a definite integral. The region of the area we just calculated is depicted in Figure 5.28. Note that the region between the curve and the x-axis is all below the x-axis. Area is always positive, but a definite integral can still produce a negative number (a net signed area). For example, if this were a profit function, a negative number indicates the company is operating at a loss over the given interval.

title: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2
snippet: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2: Evaluate the following integral using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2: {\int_{1}^{9}\frac{x - 1}{\sqrt{x}}}dx. First, eliminate the radical by...
body_xml: Evaluate the following integral using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2: $${\int_{1}^{9}\frac{x - 1}{\sqrt{x}}}dx.$$ First, eliminate the radical by rewriting the integral using rational exponents. Then, separate the numerator terms by writing each one over the denominator: $${\int_{1}^{9}{\frac{x - 1}{x^{1/2}}dx}} = {\int_{1}^{9}{\left( {\frac{x}{x^{1/2}} - \frac{1}{x^{1/2}}} \right)dx}}.$$ Use the properties of exponents to simplify: $${\int_{1}^{9}{\left( {\frac{x}{x^{1/2}} - \frac{1}{x^{1/2}}} \right)dx}} = {\int_{1}^{9}{\left( {x^{1/2} - x^{-1/2}} \right)dx}}.$$ Now, integrate using the power rule: $$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\int_{1}^{9}{\left( {x^{1/2} - x^{- {1/2}}} \right)dx}} & {= \left. \left( {\frac{x^{3/2}}{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{x^{1/2}}{\frac{1}{2}}} \right) \right|_{1}^{9}} \\ & \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{(9)^{3/2}}{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{(9)^{1/2}}{\frac{1}{2}}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{(1)^{3/2}}{\frac{3}{2}} - \frac{(1)^{1/2}}{\frac{1}{2}}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}(27) - 2(3)} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}(1) - 2(1)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= 18 - 6 - \frac{2}{3} + 2} \\ & {= \frac{40}{3}.} \end{array}$$ See Figure 5.29.

title: A Roller-Skating Race
snippet: A Roller-Skating Race: James and Kathy are racing on roller skates. They race along a long, straight track, and whoever has gone the farthest after 5 sec wins a prize. If James can skate at a velocity of f(t) = 5 + 2t ft/sec and Kathy can...
body_xml:
<example number="5.22" title="A Roller-Skating Race">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>James and Kathy are racing on roller skates. They race along a long, straight track, and whoever has gone the farthest after 5 sec wins a prize. If James can skate at a velocity of $$f(t) = 5 + 2t$$ ft/sec and Kathy can skate at a velocity of $$g(t) = 10 + \cos \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)$$ ft/sec, who is going to win the race?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We need to integrate both functions over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,5} \right\rbrack$$ and see which value is bigger. For James, we want to calculate</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{0}^{5}{\left( {5 + 2t} \right)dt}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using the power rule, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{5}{\left( {5 + 2t} \right)dt}} & {= \left. \left( {5t + t^{2}} \right) \right|_{0}^{5}} \\ & {= \left( {25 + 25} \right) = 50.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, James has skated 50 ft after 5 sec. Turning now to Kathy, we want to calculate</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{0}^{5}10} + \cos \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)dt.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We know $$\sin t$$ is an antiderivative of $$\cos t,$$ so it is reasonable to expect that an antiderivative of $$\cos \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)$$ would involve $$\sin \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right).$$ However, when we differentiate $$\sin \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right),$$ we get $$\frac{\pi}{2}\cos \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)$$ as a result of the chain rule, so we have to account for this additional coefficient when we integrate. We obtain</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{0}^{5}10} + \cos \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)dt} & {= \left. \left( {10t + \frac{2}{\pi}\sin \left( {\frac{\pi}{2}t} \right)} \right) \right|_{0}^{5}} \\ & {= \left( {50 + \frac{2}{\pi}} \right) - \left( {0 - \frac{2}{\pi}\sin 0} \right)} \\ & {\approx 50.6.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Kathy has skated approximately 50.6 ft after 5 sec. Kathy wins, but not by much!</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Integrating a Function Using the Power Rule
snippet: Integrating a Function Using the Power Rule: Use the power rule to integrate the function {\int_{1}^{4}{\sqrt{t}\left( {1 + t} \right)dt}}. The first step is to rewrite the function and simplify it so we can apply the power rule:...
body_xml:
<example number="5.23" title="Integrating a Function Using the Power Rule">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use the power rule to integrate the function $${\int_{1}^{4}{\sqrt{t}\left( {1 + t} \right)dt}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first step is to rewrite the function and simplify it so we can apply the power rule:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{1}^{4}{\sqrt{t}(1 + t)dt}} & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{t^{1/2}(1 + t)dt}}} \\ & \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {t^{1/2} + t^{3/2}} \right)dt}}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now apply the power rule:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {t^{1/2} + t^{3/2}} \right)dt}} & {= \left. \left( {\frac{2}{3}t^{3/2} + \frac{2}{5}t^{5/2}} \right) \right|_{1}^{4}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}{(4)}^{3/2} + \frac{2}{5}{(4)}^{5/2}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}{(1)}^{3/2} + \frac{2}{5}{(1)}^{5/2}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{256}{15}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.6" title="Net Change Theorem">
    <heading level="4">Net Change Theorem</heading>
    <paragraph>The new value of a changing quantity equals the initial value plus the integral of the rate of change:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} \\ \\ {F(b) = F(a) + {\int_{a}^{b}{F\prime(x)dx}}} \\ \text{or} \\ {{\int_{a}^{b}{F\prime(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)}}.} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Finding Net Displacement
snippet: Finding Net Displacement: Given a velocity function v(t) = 3t - 5 (in meters per second) for a particle in motion from time t = 0 to time t = 3, find the net displacement of the particle. Applying the net change theorem, we have...
body_xml: Given a velocity function $$v(t) = 3t - 5$$ (in meters per second) for a particle in motion from time $$t = 0$$ to time $$t = 3,$$ find the net displacement of the particle. Applying the net change theorem, we have $$\begin{array}{ll} {\int_{0}^{3}{\left( {3t - 5} \right)dt}} & {= \frac{3t^{2}}{2} - 5t|_{0}^{3}} \\ & \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{3(3)^{2}}{2} - 5(3)} \right\rbrack - 0} \\ & {= \frac{27}{2} - 15} \\ & {= \frac{27}{2} - \frac{30}{2}} \\ & {= - \frac{3}{2}.} \end{array}$$ The net displacement is $$- \frac{3}{2}$$ m (Figure 5.33).

title: Finding the Total Distance Traveled
snippet: Finding the Total Distance Traveled: Use Example 5.24 to find the total distance traveled by a particle according to the velocity function v(t) = 3t - 5 m/sec over a time interval \left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack. The total distance...
body_xml:
<example number="5.25" title="Finding the Total Distance Traveled">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use Example 5.24 to find the total distance traveled by a particle according to the velocity function $$v(t) = 3t - 5$$ m/sec over a time interval $$\left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The total distance traveled includes both the positive and the negative values. Therefore, we must integrate the absolute value of the velocity function to find the total distance traveled.</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To continue with the example, use two integrals to find the total distance. First, find the t-intercept of the function, since that is where the division of the interval occurs. Set the equation equal to zero and solve for t. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} {3t - 5} & = & 0 \\ {3t} & = & 5 \\ t & = & {\frac{5}{3}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The two subintervals are $$\left\lbrack {0,\frac{5}{3}} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack {\frac{5}{3},3} \right\rbrack.$$ To find the total distance traveled, integrate the absolute value of the function. Since the function is negative over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,\frac{5}{3}} \right\rbrack,$$ we have $$\left| {v(t)} \right| = -v(t)$$ over that interval. Over $$\left\lbrack {\frac{5}{3},3} \right\rbrack,$$ the function is positive, so $$\left| {v(t)} \right| = v(t).$$ Thus, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\int_{0}^{3}{\left| {v(t)} \right|dt}} & {= {\int_{0}^{5/3}{-v(t)dt + {\int_{5/3}^{3}v}(t)dt}}} \\ & \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{5/3}5} - 3tdt + {\int_{5/3}^{3}3}t - 5dt} \\ & {= \left. \left( {5t - \frac{3t^{2}}{2}} \right) \right|_{0}^{5/3} + \left. \left( {\frac{3t^{2}}{2} - 5t} \right) \right|_{5/3}^{3}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {5\left( \frac{5}{3} \right) - \frac{3\left( {5/3} \right)^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack - 0 + \left\lbrack {\frac{27}{2} - 15} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{3\left( {5/3} \right)^{2}}{2} - \frac{25}{3}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{25}{3} - \frac{25}{6} + \frac{27}{2} - 15 - \frac{25}{6} + \frac{25}{3}} \\ & {= \frac{41}{6}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>So, the total distance traveled is $$\frac{41}{6}$$ m.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: How Many Gallons of Gasoline Are Consumed?
snippet: How Many Gallons of Gasoline Are Consumed?: If the motor on a motorboat is started at t = 0 and the boat consumes gasoline at the rate of 5 - 0.1t^{3} gal/hr, how much gasoline is used in the first 2 hours? Express the problem as a...
body_xml:
<example number="5.26" title="How Many Gallons of Gasoline Are Consumed?">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>If the motor on a motorboat is started at $$t = 0$$ and the boat consumes gasoline at the rate of $$5 - 0.1t^{3}$$ gal/hr, how much gasoline is used in the first 2 hours?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Express the problem as a definite integral, integrate, and evaluate using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The limits of integration are the endpoints of the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,2} \right\rbrack.$$ We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{0}^{2}\left( 5 - 0.1t^{3} \right)dt = \left( 5t-0.1\frac{t^{4}}{4} \right)\left. \middle| {}_{2} \right._{0} = \left\lbrack 5(2)-0.1\frac{(2)^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack -0 = 10-0.4 = 9.6$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus, the motorboat uses 9.6 gal of gas in 2 hours.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Chapter Opener: Iceboats
snippet: Chapter Opener: Iceboats: As we saw at the beginning of the chapter, top iceboat racers (Figure 5.1) can attain speeds of up to five times the wind speed. Andrew is an intermediate iceboater, though, so he attains speeds equal to only...
body_xml: As we saw at the beginning of the chapter, top iceboat racers (Figure 5.1) can attain speeds of up to five times the wind speed. Andrew is an intermediate iceboater, though, so he attains speeds equal to only twice the wind speed. Suppose Andrew takes his iceboat out one morning when a light 5-mph breeze has been blowing all morning. As Andrew gets his iceboat set up, though, the wind begins to pick up. During his first half hour of iceboating, the wind speed increases according to the function $$v(t) = 20t + 5.$$ For the second half hour of Andrew’s outing, the wind remains steady at 15 mph. In other words, the wind speed is given by $$v(t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} {20t + 5} & \text{for} & {0 \leq t \leq \frac{1}{2}} \\ 15 & \text{for} & {\frac{1}{2} \leq t \leq 1.} \end{array} \right.$$ Recalling that Andrew’s iceboat travels at twice the wind speed, and assuming he moves in a straight line away from his starting point, how far is Andrew from his starting point after 1 hour? To figure out how far Andrew has traveled, we need to integrate his velocity, which is twice the wind speed. Then Distance $$= {\int_{0}^{1}{2v(t)dt}}.$$ Substituting the expressions we were given for $$v(t),$$ we get $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{1}{2v(t)dt}} & {= {\int_{0}^{1/2}{2v(t)dt + {\int_{1/2}^{1}{2v(t)dt}}}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1/2}{2\left( {20t + 5} \right)dt + {\int_{1/2}^{1}{2(15)dt}}}}} \\ & {= {\int_{0}^{1/2}{\left( {40t + 10} \right)dt + {\int_{1/2}^{1}{30dt}}}}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {20t^{2} + 10t} \right\rbrack{|_{0}^{1/2} + \left\lbrack {30t} \right\rbrack|_{1/2}^{1}}} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{20}{4} + 5} \right) - 0 + \left( {30 - 15} \right)} \\ & {= 25.} \end{array}$$ Andrew is 25 mi from his starting point after 1 hour.

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Integrals of Even and Odd Functions" title="Rule: Integrals of Even and Odd Functions">
    <paragraph>For continuous even functions such that $$f\left( {-x} \right) = f(x),$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{-a}^{a}{f(x)dx = 2{\int_{0}^{a}{f(x)dx}}}}.$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For continuous odd functions such that $$f\left( {-x} \right) = -f(x),$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{-a}^{a}{f(x)dx = 0}}.$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Integrating an Even Function
snippet: Integrating an Even Function: Integrate the even function \int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {3x^{8} - 2} \right)dx} and verify that the integration formula for even functions holds. The symmetry appears in the graphs in Figure 5.35. Graph (a) shows the...
body_xml: Integrate the even function $$\int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {3x^{8} - 2} \right)dx}$$ and verify that the integration formula for even functions holds. The symmetry appears in the graphs in Figure 5.35. Graph (a) shows the region below the curve and above the x-axis. We have to zoom in to this graph by a huge amount to see the region. Graph (b) shows the region above the curve and below the x-axis. The signed area of this region is negative. Both views illustrate the symmetry about the y-axis of an even function. We have $$\begin{array}{ll} {\int_{-2}^{2}{\left( {3x^{8} - 2} \right)dx}} & {= \left( {\frac{x^{9}}{3} - 2x} \right)|_{-2}^{2}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \left\lbrack {\frac{(2)^{9}}{3} - 2(2)} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{(-2)^{9}}{3} - 2(-2)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{512}{3} - 4} \right) - \left( {- \frac{512}{3} + 4} \right)} \\ & {= \frac{1000}{3}.} \end{array}$$ To verify the integration formula for even functions, we can calculate the integral from 0 to 2 and double it, then check to make sure we get the same answer. $$\begin{array}{ll} {\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {3x^{8} - 2} \right)dx}} & {= \left( {\frac{x^{9}}{3} - 2x} \right)|_{0}^{2}} \\ & \\ & {= \frac{512}{3} - 4} \\ & {= \frac{500}{3}} \end{array}$$ Since $$2 \cdot \frac{500}{3} = \frac{1000}{3},$$ we have verified the formula for even functions in this particular example.

title: Integrating an Odd Function
snippet: Integrating an Odd Function: Evaluate the definite integral of the odd function -5\sin x over the interval \left\lbrack {-\pi,\pi} \right\rbrack. The graph is shown in Figure 5.36. We can see the symmetry about the origin by the positive...
body_xml: Evaluate the definite integral of the odd function $$-5\sin x$$ over the interval $$\left\lbrack {-\pi,\pi} \right\rbrack.$$ The graph is shown in Figure 5.36. We can see the symmetry about the origin by the positive area above the x-axis over $$\left\lbrack {-\pi,0} \right\rbrack,$$ and the negative area below the x-axis over $$\left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack.$$ We have $$\begin{array}{ll} {\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}{-5\sin xdx}} & {= -5\left( {-\cos x} \right)|_{-\pi}^{\pi}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= 5\cos x|_{-\pi}^{\pi}} \\ & {= \left\lbrack {5\cos \pi} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {5\cos \left( {-\pi} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= -5 - (-5)} \\ & {= 0.} \end{array}$$

snippet: Substitution with Indefinite Integrals: Substitution with Indefinite Integrals Let u = g(x), where g^{\prime}\left. (x \right) is continuous over an interval, let f(x) be continuous over the corresponding range of g, and let F(x) be an...

<note type="theorem_key" source_type="theorem" number="5.7" title="Substitution with Indefinite Integrals">
    <heading level="3">Substitution with Indefinite Integrals</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$u = g(x),$$ where $$g^{\prime}\left. (x \right)$$ is continuous over an interval, let $$f(x)$$ be continuous over the corresponding range of g, and let $$F(x)$$ be an antiderivative of $$f(x).$$ Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \left. \int{f\left\lbrack {g(x)} \right\rbrack g^{\prime}\left. (x \right)dx} \right. & {= {\int f}(u)du} \\ & {= F(u) + C} \\ & {= F\left( {g(x)} \right) + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Problem-Solving Strategy
snippet: Problem-Solving Strategy: Integration by Substitution Look carefully at the integrand and select an expression g(x) within the integrand to set equal to u. Let’s select g(x) such that g^{\prime}\left. (x \right) is also part of the...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="Problem-Solving Strategy" title="Problem-Solving Strategy">
    <heading level="4">Integration by Substitution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Look carefully at the integrand and select an expression $$g(x)$$ within the integrand to set equal to u. Let’s select $$g(x)$$ such that $$g^{\prime}\left. (x \right)$$ is also part of the integrand.</item>
      <item>Substitute $$u = g(x)$$ and $$du = g^{\prime}\left. (x \right)dx$$ into the integral.</item>
      <item>We should now be able to evaluate the integral with respect to u. If the integral can’t be evaluated we need to go back and select a different expression to use as u.</item>
      <item>Evaluate the integral in terms of u.</item>
      <item>Write the result in terms of x and the expression $$g(x).$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Using Substitution to Find an Antiderivative
snippet: Using Substitution to Find an Antiderivative: Use substitution to find the antiderivative \left. \int{6x\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{4}dx} \right.. The first step is to choose an expression for u. We choose u = 3x^{2} + 4 because then du =...
body_xml:
<example number="5.30" title="Using Substitution to Find an Antiderivative">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to find the antiderivative $$\left. \int{6x\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{4}dx} \right..$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>The first step is to choose an expression for u. We choose $$u = 3x^{2} + 4$$ because then $$du = 6xdx,$$ and we already have du in the integrand. Write the integral in terms of u:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int{6x\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{4}dx} \right. = {\int{u^{4}du}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Remember that du is the derivative of the expression chosen for u, regardless of what is inside the integrand. Now we can evaluate the integral with respect to u:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} \left. \int{u^{4}du} \right. & {= \frac{u^{5}}{5} + C} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \frac{\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{5}}{5} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
    <paragraph>We can check our answer by taking the derivative of the result of integration. We should obtain the integrand. Picking a value for C of 1, we let $$y = \frac{1}{5}\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{5} + 1.$$ We have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = \frac{1}{5}\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{5} + 1,$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ y^{\prime} & {= \left( \frac{1}{5} \right)5\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{4}6x} \\ & {= 6x\left( {3x^{2} + 4} \right)^{4}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>This is exactly the expression we started with inside the integrand.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Using Substitution with Alteration
snippet: Using Substitution with Alteration: Use substitution to find \left. \int{z\sqrt{z^{2} - 5}dz} \right.. Rewrite the integral as \left. \int{z\left( {z^{2} - 5} \right)^{1/2}dz} \right.. Let u = z^{2} - 5 and du = 2z dz. Now we have a...
body_xml:
<example number="5.31" title="Using Substitution with Alteration">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to find $$\left. \int{z\sqrt{z^{2} - 5}dz} \right..$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Rewrite the integral as $$\left. \int{z\left( {z^{2} - 5} \right)^{1/2}dz} \right..$$ Let $$u = z^{2} - 5$$ and $$du = 2z dz.$$ Now we have a problem because $$du = 2z dz$$ and the original expression has only $$z dz.$$ We have to alter our expression for du or the integral in u will be twice as large as it should be. If we multiply both sides of the du equation by $$\frac{1}{2}.$$ we can solve this problem. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{aligned} & \\ u & {= z^{2} - 5} \\ {du} & {= 2z dz} \\ {\frac{1}{2}du} & {= \frac{1}{2}\left( {2z} \right)dz = z dz.} \end{aligned}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Write the integral in terms of u, but pull the $$\frac{1}{2}$$ outside the integration symbol:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int{z\left( {z^{2} - 5} \right)^{1/2}dz =} \right.\frac{1}{2}{\int{u^{1/2}du.}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Integrate the expression in u:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ {\frac{1}{2}{\int{u^{1/2}du}}} & {= \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\frac{u^{3/2}}{\frac{3}{2}} + C} \\ & \\ & {= \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)u^{3/2} + C} \\ & {= \frac{1}{3}u^{3/2} + C} \\ & {= \frac{1}{3}\left( {z^{2} - 5} \right)^{3/2} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Using Substitution with Integrals of Trigonometric Functions
snippet: Using Substitution with Integrals of Trigonometric Functions: Use substitution to evaluate the integral \left. \int{\frac{\sin t}{\cos^{3}t}dt} \right.. We know the derivative of \cos t is -\sin t, so we set u = \cos t. Then du = -\sin...
body_xml:
<example number="5.32" title="Using Substitution with Integrals of Trigonometric Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to evaluate the integral $$\left. \int{\frac{\sin t}{\cos^{3}t}dt} \right..$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We know the derivative of $$\cos t$$ is $$-\sin t,$$ so we set $$u = \cos t.$$ Then $$du = -\sin tdt.$$ Substituting into the integral, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int{\frac{\sin t}{\cos^{3}t}dt = -\left. \int\frac{du}{u^{3}} \right.} \right..$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Evaluating the integral, we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {-\left. \int\frac{du}{u^{3}} \right.} & {= -{\int{u^{-3}du}}} \\ & {= -\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)u^{-2} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Putting the answer back in terms of t, we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \left. \int{\frac{\sin t}{\cos^{3}t}dt} \right. & {= \frac{1}{2u^{2}} + C} \\ & \\ & {= \frac{1}{2\cos^{2}t} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding an Antiderivative Using u-Substitution
snippet: Finding an Antiderivative Using u-Substitution: Use substitution to find the antiderivative \left. \int{\frac{x}{\sqrt{x - 1}}dx.} \right. If we let u = x - 1, then du = dx. But this does not account for the x in the numerator of the...
body_xml:
<example number="5.33" title="Finding an Antiderivative Using u-Substitution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to find the antiderivative $$\left. \int{\frac{x}{\sqrt{x - 1}}dx.} \right.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>If we let $$u = x - 1,$$ then $$du = dx.$$ But this does not account for the x in the numerator of the integrand. We need to express x in terms of u. If $$u = x - 1,$$ then $$x = u + 1.$$ Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of u:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} \left. \int{\frac{x}{\sqrt{x - 1}}dx} \right. & {= \left. \int{\frac{u + 1}{\sqrt{u}}du} \right.} \\ & \\ & {= \left. \int{\sqrt{u} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}du} \right.} \\ & {= \left. \int{\left( {u^{1/2} + u^{-1/2}} \right)du} \right..} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we integrate in the usual way, replace u with the original expression, and factor and simplify the result. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} \left. \int{\left( {u^{1/2} + u^{-1/2}} \right)du} \right. & {= \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + 2u^{1/2} + C} \\ & \\ & {= \frac{2}{3}\left( {x - 1} \right)^{3/2} + 2\left( {x - 1} \right)^{1/2} + C} \\ & {= \left( {x - 1} \right)^{1/2}\left\lbrack {\frac{2}{3}\left( {x - 1} \right) + 2} \right\rbrack + C} \\ & {= \left( {x - 1} \right)^{1/2}{\left( {\frac{2}{3}x - \frac{2}{3} + \frac{6}{3}} \right) + C}} \\ & {= \left( {x - 1} \right)^{1/2}{\left( {\frac{2}{3}x + \frac{4}{3}} \right) + C}} \\ & {= \frac{2}{3}\left( {x - 1} \right)^{1/2}\left( {x + 2} \right) + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<example number="5.34" title="Using Substitution to Evaluate a Definite Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to evaluate $${\int_{0}^{1}{x^{2}\left( {1 + 2x^{3}} \right)^{5}}}dx.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$u = 1 + 2x^{3},$$ so $$du = 6x^{2}dx.$$ Since the original function includes one factor of x2 and $$du = 6x^{2}dx,$$ multiply both sides of the du equation by $$1/6.$$ Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {du} & = & {6x^{2}dx} \\ {\frac{1}{6}du} & = & {x^{2}dx.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>To adjust the limits of integration, note that when $$x = 0,u = 1 + 2(0) = 1,$$ and when $$x = 1,u = 1 + 2(1) = 3.$$ Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{0}^{1}{x^{2}\left( {1 + 2x^{3}} \right)^{5}dx = \frac{1}{6}{\int_{1}^{3}{u^{5}du}}}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Evaluating this expression, we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\frac{1}{6}{\int_{1}^{3}{u^{5}du}}} & {= \left( \frac{1}{6} \right)\left( \frac{u^{6}}{6} \right)|_{1}^{3}} \\ & {= \frac{1}{36}\left\lbrack {(3)^{6} - (1)^{6}} \right\rbrack} \\ & {= \frac{182}{9}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Using Substitution to Evaluate a Trigonometric Integral: Use substitution to evaluate {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos^{2}\theta d\theta}}. Let us first use a trigonometric identity to rewrite the integral. The trig identity \cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1...
body_xml:
<example number="5.36" title="Using Substitution to Evaluate a Trigonometric Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to evaluate $${\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos^{2}\theta d\theta}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let us first use a trigonometric identity to rewrite the integral. The trig identity $$\cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}$$ allows us to rewrite the integral as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos^{2}\theta d\theta}} = {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}d\theta.}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left( \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2} \right)}d\theta} & {= {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\left( {\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2\theta} \right)d\theta}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{d\theta}} + \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos 2\theta d\theta.}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>We can evaluate the first integral as it is, but we need to make a substitution to evaluate the second integral. Let $$u = 2\theta.$$ Then, $$du = 2d\theta,$$ or $$\frac{1}{2}du = d\theta.$$ Also, when $$\theta = 0,u = 0,$$ and when $$\theta = \pi/2,u = \pi.$$ Expressing the second integral in terms of u, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{d\theta + \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\cos 2\theta d\theta}}}}} & {= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{d\theta + \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right){\int_{0}^{\pi}{\cos udu}}}}} \\ & {= \frac{\theta}{2}{|_{\theta = 0}^{\theta = \pi/2} + \frac{1}{4}\sin u|_{u = 0}^{u = \pi}}} \\ & {= \left( {\frac{\pi}{4} - 0} \right) + \left( {0 - 0} \right) = \frac{\pi}{4}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Square Root of an Exponential Function: Find the antiderivative of the exponential function e^{x}\sqrt{1 + e^{x}}. First rewrite the problem using a rational exponent: \left. \int{e^{x}\sqrt{1 + e^{x}}} \right.dx = \left. \int{e^{x}\left(...
body_xml: Find the antiderivative of the exponential function $$e^{x}\sqrt{1 + e^{x}}.$$ First rewrite the problem using a rational exponent: $$\left. \int{e^{x}\sqrt{1 + e^{x}}} \right.dx = \left. \int{e^{x}\left( {1 + e^{x}} \right)^{1/2}dx} \right..$$ Using substitution, choose $$u = 1 + e^{x}.$$ Then, $$du = e^{x}dx.$$ We have (Figure 5.37) $$\left. \int{e^{x}\left( {1 + e^{x}} \right)^{1/2}dx = \left. \int{u^{1/2}du} \right.} \right..$$ Then $$\left. \int{u^{1/2}du = \frac{u^{3/2}}{3/2} + C} \right. = \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + C = \frac{2}{3}\left( {1 + e^{x}} \right)^{3/2} + C.$$

<example number="5.39" title="Using Substitution with an Exponential Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Use substitution to evaluate the indefinite integral $$\int{3x^{2}e^{2x^{3}}dx.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Here we choose to let u equal the expression in the exponent on e. Let $$u = 2x^{3}$$ and $$du = 6x^{2}dx..$$ Again, du is off by a constant multiplier; the original function contains a factor of 3x2, not 6x2. Multiply both sides of the equation by $$\frac{1}{2}$$ so that the integrand in u equals the integrand in x. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int{3x^{2}e^{2x^{3}}} \right.dx = \frac{1}{2}{\int{e^{u}du}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Integrate the expression in u and then substitute the original expression in x back into the u integral:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{1}{2}{\int e^{u}}du = \frac{1}{2}e^{u} + C = \frac{1}{2}e^{2x^{3}} + C.$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

title: Finding a Price–Demand Equation
snippet: Finding a Price–Demand Equation: Find the price–demand equation for a particular brand of toothpaste at a supermarket chain when the demand is 50 tubes per week at \$2.35 per tube, given that the marginal price—demand function,...
body_xml:
<example number="5.40" title="Finding a Price–Demand Equation">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the price–demand equation for a particular brand of toothpaste at a supermarket chain when the demand is 50 tubes per week at \$2.35 per tube, given that the marginal price—demand function, $$p^{\prime}\left. (x \right),$$ for x number of tubes per week, is given as</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$p'(x) = -0.015e^{-0.01x}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If the supermarket chain sells 100 tubes per week, what price should it set?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>To find the price–demand equation, integrate the marginal price–demand function. First find the antiderivative, then look at the particulars. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {p(x)} & {= \left. \int{-0.015e^{-0.01x}dx} \right.} \\ & {= -0.015\left. \int e^{-0.01x} \right.dx.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Using substitution, let $$u = -0.01x$$ and $$du = -0.01dx.$$ Then, divide both sides of the du equation by −0.01. This gives</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\frac{-0.015}{-0.01}\left. \int{e^{u}du} \right.} & {= 1.5\left. \int{e^{u}du} \right.} \\ & \\ & {= 1.5e^{u} + C} \\ & {= 1.5e^{-0.01x} + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The next step is to solve for C. We know that when the price is \$2.35 per tube, the demand is 50 tubes per week. This means</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {p(50)} & {= 1.5e^{-0.01(50)} + C} \\ & {= 2.35.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Now, just solve for C:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ C & {= 2.35 - 1.5e^{-0.5}} \\ & {= 2.35 - 0.91} \\ & {= 1.44.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$p(x) = 1.5e^{-0.01x} + 1.44.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>If the supermarket sells 100 tubes of toothpaste per week, the price would be</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$p(100) = 1.5e^{-0.01(100)} + 1.44 = 1.5e^{-1} + 1.44 \approx 1.99.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>The supermarket should charge \$1.99 per tube if it is selling 100 tubes per week.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Evaluating a Definite Integral Involving an Exponential Function: Evaluate the definite integral {\int_{1}^{2}{e^{1 - x}dx}}. Again, substitution is the method to use. Let u = 1 - x, so du = -1dx or -du = dx. Then {\int{e^{1 - x}dx =...
body_xml: Evaluate the definite integral $${\int_{1}^{2}{e^{1 - x}dx}}.$$ Again, substitution is the method to use. Let $$u = 1 - x,$$ so $$du = -1dx$$ or $$-du = dx.$$ Then $${\int{e^{1 - x}dx = -{\int{e^{u}du}}}}.$$ Next, change the limits of integration. Using the equation $$u = 1 - x,$$ we have $$\begin{array}{l} {u = 1 - (1) = 0} \\ {u = 1 - (2) = -1.} \end{array}$$ The integral then becomes $$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{1}^{2}{e^{1 - x}dx}} & {= -{\int_{0}^{-1}{e^{u}du}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= {\int_{-1}^{0}{e^{u}du}}} \\ & {= \left. e^{u} \right|_{-1}^{0}} \\ & {= e^{0} - \left( e^{-1} \right)} \\ & {= -e^{-1} + 1.} \end{array}$$ See Figure 5.38.

snippet: Growth of Bacteria in a Culture: Suppose the rate of growth of bacteria in a Petri dish is given by q(t) = 3^{t}, where t is given in hours and q(t) is given in thousands of bacteria per hour. If a culture starts with 10,000 bacteria, find...
body_xml:
<example number="5.42" title="Growth of Bacteria in a Culture">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose the rate of growth of bacteria in a Petri dish is given by $$q(t) = 3^{t},$$ where t is given in hours and $$q(t)$$ is given in thousands of bacteria per hour. If a culture starts with 10,000 bacteria, find a function $$Q(t)$$ that gives the number of bacteria in the Petri dish at any time t. How many bacteria are in the dish after 2 hours?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$Q(t) = {\int{3^{t}dt = \frac{3^{t}}{\ln 3} + C.}}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then, at $$t = 0$$ we have $$Q(0) = 10 = \frac{1}{\ln 3} + C,$$ so $$C \approx 9.090$$ and we get</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$Q(t) = \frac{3^{t}}{\ln 3} + 9.090.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>At time $$t = 2,$$ we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$Q(2) = \frac{3^{2}}{\ln 3} + 9.090$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$= 17.282.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>After 2 hours, there are 17,282 bacteria in the dish.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Fruit Fly Population Growth: Suppose a population of fruit flies increases at a rate of g(t) = 2e^{0.02t}, in flies per day. If the initial population of fruit flies is 100 flies, how many flies are in the population after 10 days? Let...
body_xml:
<example number="5.43" title="Fruit Fly Population Growth">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Suppose a population of fruit flies increases at a rate of $$g(t) = 2e^{0.02t},$$ in flies per day. If the initial population of fruit flies is 100 flies, how many flies are in the population after 10 days?</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>Let $$G(t)$$ represent the number of flies in the population at time t. Applying the net change theorem, we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {G(10)} & {= G(0) + \int_{0}^{10}2e^{0.02t}dt} \\ & {= 100 + \left. \left\lbrack {\frac{2}{0.02}e^{0.02t}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{10}} \\ & {= 100 + \left. \left\lbrack {100e^{0.02t}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{10}} \\ & {= 100 + 100e^{0.2} - 100} \\ & {\approx 122.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>There are 122 flies in the population after 10 days.</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Substitution: Evaluate the definite integral using substitution: {\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{e^{1/x}}{x^{2}}dx}}. This problem requires some rewriting to simplify applying the properties. First, rewrite the...

<example number="5.44" title="Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Substitution">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate the definite integral using substitution: $${\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{e^{1/x}}{x^{2}}dx}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This problem requires some rewriting to simplify applying the properties. First, rewrite the exponent on e as a power of x, then bring the x2 in the denominator up to the numerator using a negative exponent. We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{e^{1/x}}{x^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{e^{x^{-1}}x^{-2}dx}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Let $$u = x^{-1},$$ the exponent on e. Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{aligned} {du} & {= -x^{-2}dx} \\ {- du} & {= x^{-2}dx.} \end{aligned}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Bringing the negative sign outside the integral sign, the problem now reads</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$-{\int{e^{u}du}}.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Next, change the limits of integration:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} \\ \\ {u = {(1)}^{-1} = 1} \\ {u = {(2)}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Notice that now the limits begin with the larger number, meaning we must multiply by −1 and interchange the limits. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} & \\ & \\ & \\ {-{\int_{1}^{1/2}{e^{u}du}}} & {= {\int_{1/2}^{1}{e^{u}du}}} \\ & {= e^{u}|_{1/2}^{1}} \\ & {= e - e^{1/2}} \\ & {= e - \sqrt{e}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Integration Formulas Involving Logarithmic Functions" title="Rule: Integration Formulas Involving Logarithmic Functions">
    <paragraph>The following formulas can be used to evaluate integrals involving logarithmic functions.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} \left. \int{x^{-1}dx} \right. & = & {\ln |x| + C} \\ {{\int\ln } x dx} & = & {x\ln x - x + C = x\left( {\ln x - 1} \right) + C} \\ {{\int\log_{a}}x dx} & = & {\frac{x}{\ln a}\left( {\ln x - 1} \right) + C} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

snippet: Finding an Antiderivative of a Rational Function: Find the antiderivative of \frac{2x^{3} + 3x}{x^{4} + 3x^{2}}. This can be rewritten as \left. \int{\left( {2x^{3} + 3x} \right)\left( {x^{4} + 3x^{2}} \right)^{-1}dx} \right.. Use...
body_xml:
<example number="5.46" title="Finding an Antiderivative of a Rational Function">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the antiderivative of $$\frac{2x^{3} + 3x}{x^{4} + 3x^{2}}.$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>This can be rewritten as $$\left. \int{\left( {2x^{3} + 3x} \right)\left( {x^{4} + 3x^{2}} \right)^{-1}dx} \right..$$ Use substitution. Let $$u = x^{4} + 3x^{2},$$ then $$du = 4x^{3} + 6x.$$ Alter du by factoring out the 2. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cll} & & \\ {du} & = & {\left( {4x^{3} + 6x} \right)dx} \\ & = & {2\left( {2x^{3} + 3x} \right)dx} \\ {\frac{1}{2} du} & = & {\left( {2x^{3} + 3x} \right)dx.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Rewrite the integrand in u:</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int{\left( {2x^{3} + 3x} \right)\left( {x^{4} + 3x^{2}} \right)^{-1}dx} \right. = \frac{1}{2}\left. \int u^{-1} \right.du.$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then we have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ll} {\frac{1}{2}\left. \int{u^{-1}du} \right.} & {= \frac{1}{2}\ln |u| + C} \\ & \\ & {= \frac{1}{2}\ln \left| {x^{4} + 3x^{2}} \right| + C.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

snippet: Evaluating a Definite Integral: Find the definite integral of \int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}dx.} We need substitution to evaluate this problem. Let u = 1 + \cos x,, so du = -\sin x dx. Rewrite the integral in terms of u,...

<example number="5.48" title="Evaluating a Definite Integral">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Find the definite integral of $$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}{\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}dx.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We need substitution to evaluate this problem. Let $$u = 1 + \cos x,,$$ so $$du = -\sin x dx.$$ Rewrite the integral in terms of u, changing the limits of integration as well. Thus,</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {u = 1 + \cos (0) = 2} \\ {u = 1 + \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} \right) = 1.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
      <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} {\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}} & {= -{\int_{2}^{1}{u^{-1}du}}} \\ & \\ & \\ & {= {\int_{1}^{2}{u^{-1}du}}} \\ & {= \left. {\ln |u|} \right|_{1}^{2}} \\ & {= \lbrack\ln 2 - \ln 1\rbrack} \\ & {= \ln 2.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

<note type="rule" source_type="Rule: Integration Formulas Resulting in Inverse Trigonometric Functions" title="Rule: Integration Formulas Resulting in Inverse Trigonometric Functions">
    <paragraph>The following integration formulas yield inverse trigonometric functions. Assume $$a > 0$$ :</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\left. \int\frac{du}{\sqrt{a^{2} - u^{2}}} = \sin^{- 1}\left( \frac{u}{a} \right)+C \right.$$ (5.23)</item>
      <item>$$\left. \int\frac{du}{a^{2} + u^{2}} \right. = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{a} + C$$ (5.24)</item>
      <item>$$\left. \int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^{2} - a^{2}}} = \frac{1}{a}\sec^{-1}\frac{|u|}{a} + C \right.$$ (5.25)</item>
    </list>
  </note>

<example number="5.49" title="Evaluating a Definite Integral Using Inverse Trigonometric Functions">
    <problem>
      <paragraph>Evaluate the definite integral $$\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}.}$$</paragraph>
    </problem>
    <solution>
      <paragraph>We can go directly to the formula for the antiderivative in the rule on integration formulas resulting in inverse trigonometric functions, and then evaluate the definite integral. We have</paragraph>
      <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{cl} & \\ & \\ {\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}} & {= \sin^{-1}x|_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}} \\ & {= \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} - \sin^{-1}0} \\ & {= \frac{\pi}{6} - 0} \\ & {= \frac{\pi}{6}.} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    </solution>
  </example>

      <paragraph math="block">$$\left. \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4 - 9x^{2}}} \right. = \frac{1}{3}\left. \int\frac{du}{\sqrt{4 - u^{2}}} \right..$$</paragraph>
